[P117] Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-lag Effect in Stock Returns (Kewei Hou, 2007, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 601, read from: full text (your PDF, working paper version))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/revfin/hhm003
Question: How do stock returns of linked companies (same industry) move relative to each other when news hits, and can the delay be traded?
Data: US (NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ), July 1963 to December 2001, all publicly traded firms with sharecodes 10 or 11, CRSP, COMPUSTAT, S&P, I/B/E/S
Method: Decompose lead lag into intra- and inter industry components using weekly returns and size/characteristic sorts; test predictability of small/low characteristic firms by lagged returns of big/high characteristic firms within same industry.
Findings:
  * Within an industry, last week's returns of big firms predict this week's returns of small firms, but not the other way round: sum of four weekly lag coefficients 0.2304 (significant at 1%) against 0.0294 (not significant) for big firms of other industries (Intra- versus Inter-Industry Lead-Lag Effects panel)
  * The effect is driven by bad news: small firms' response to big firm returns is 0.2841 after negative weeks and 0.1283 after positive weeks (Good News versus Bad News panel)
  * The signal is in small stocks at a weekly horizon, and is stronger in small, volatile, less competitive and neglected industries; leaders lead followers, value firms lead growth firms, and low volatility firms lead high volatility peers
  * The intra industry lead lag drives industry momentum. The 25, 18 and 22 basis points per week (1, 6 and 12 month formation periods) are industry momentum profits, not returns of this signal
  * The paper trades no strategy: it reports regression coefficients only, with no returns after costs and no data after 2001
Strength: strong (Long sample (1963-2001), multiple robustness checks (value weighted, subperiods), significant statistical results.)
Limits: Working paper version. No strategy returns or trading costs: the results are regression coefficients on weekly returns, US 1963 to 2001. The signal sits in small stocks, where costs are highest.
For traders: Watch industry leaders for signals on smaller peers; expect delays of weeks for full price adjustment.
For the app: Feature: Prioritize news on industry leaders; link to followers with a delay warning.

[P129] Maxing Out: Stocks as Lotteries and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (Turan G. Bali, Nusret Cakici, Robert Whitelaw, 2008, SSRN Electronic Journal, cited by 1,628, read from: full text (Unpaywall repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1262416
Question: Does the negative relationship between a stock's maximum daily return in the previous month and its future returns survive trading costs, publication, and recent market data?
Data: US stock market (NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ), July 1962 to December 2005, value weighted and equal weighted decile portfolios.
Method: Sort stocks into deciles based on their maximum daily return (MAX) or average of top 5 daily returns (MAX(5)) from the previous month. Form portfolios (long low MAX, short high MAX) and measure monthly returns and risk adjusted alphas (Fama French Carhart 4-factor) over the following month.
Findings:
  * Value weighted average raw return difference between low MAX and high MAX deciles is -1.03% per month (t statistic -2.83).
  * Value weighted 4-factor alpha difference between low MAX and high MAX deciles is -1.18% per month (t statistic -4.71).
  * Equal weighted average raw return difference between low MAX and high MAX deciles is -1.11% per month after controlling for size, book to market, momentum, short term reversal, and liquidity.
  * Equal weighted average risk adjusted return difference is -1.06% per month after controls.
  * The effect is driven by the top deciles (8, 9, 10) where average returns drop from 1.00% to -0.02% per month, while lower deciles remain stable around 1.00% to 1.16%.
Strength: strong (The study uses a long sample period (43 years), robust statistical controls for known factors, and demonstrates significance in both value weighted and equal weighted portfolios.)
Limits: The sample ends in 2005, so it does not test performance in recent years or after publication; the paper explicitly states it does not calculate trading costs, noting that high MAX stocks are often small and illiquid which would increase costs; the strategy requires short selling which is difficult for retail investors.
For traders: Individual traders should avoid buying stocks that have had a massive single day gain in the last month, as they tend to underperform; however, shorting them is likely too costly and difficult for retail due to illiquidity and short sale constraints.
For the app: Add a 'Lottery Risk' filter that flags stocks with a maximum daily gain >10% in the last 21 days and suggests a 'Sell' or 'Avoid' signal, explaining that these stocks often underperform in the following month due to investor overpayment for lottery like payoffs.
Also tests (no cards written): Bivariate sorts controlling for idiosyncratic volatility; Bivariate sorts controlling for total skewness; Bivariate sorts controlling for systematic skewness; Bivariate sorts controlling for idiosyncratic skewness; Cross sectional Fama MacBeth regressions using MAX as a predictor

[P147] Can ChatGPT forecast stock price movements? Return predictability and large language models (Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Yuehua Tang, 2026, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 419, read from: full text (arXiv))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104335
Question: Can large language models like GPT-4 predict stock price movements and subsequent drift based on news headlines, and how do transaction costs and rebalancing strategies affect the profitability of these signals?
Data: US stock market, sample period October 2021 to May 2024, using news headlines and GPT-4 sentiment scores; data source includes RavenPack for news and GPT-4 API for scoring.
Method: The authors use GPT-4 to score news headlines as positive or negative. They construct long short portfolios (buying positive, selling negative) based on these scores. They test two news types: overnight news (traded open to close) and intraday news (traded close to close). They compare equal weighted and value weighted portfolios under different rebalancing frequencies (100%, 50%, 25%) and transaction cost assumptions (0, 5, 10, 20 basis points).
Findings:
  * A long short strategy based on GPT-4 scores for overnight news earns 34 basis points per day before transaction costs (2021m10 to 2024m5).
  * Without transaction costs, the cumulative return of the long short overnight strategy is around 700% from October 2021 to May 2024.
  * With a 5 basis point round trip transaction cost, the equal weighted 100% rebalancing strategy maintains a Sharpe ratio of 2.13 and a cumulative return over 300%.
  * With a 10 basis point round trip transaction cost, the equal weighted 100% rebalancing strategy's Sharpe ratio falls to 1.29, while the 25% rebalancing strategy maintains a Sharpe ratio of 1.34.
  * The strategy becomes unprofitable at 20 basis points round trip transaction costs for equal weighted 100% rebalancing (Sharpe ratio -0.394) and for all value weighted strategies even at 5 basis points.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large sample size (2.5 years of daily data), tests multiple robustness scenarios (rebalancing, costs, weighting), and provides detailed transaction cost analysis in appendices.)
Limits: The sample period is relatively short (Oct 2021-May 2024) and covers a specific market environment; the strategy relies on GPT-4 which may change over time; the paper does not test performance after 2024 or in different market regimes; the high turnover of the baseline strategy makes it difficult for retail traders to implement without significant slippage.
For traders: Individual traders can potentially use GPT-4 sentiment on news to identify short term drift, but must use partial rebalancing to reduce turnover and costs, and should focus on equal weighted portfolios of smaller stocks where the signal is strongest.
For the app: The app should implement a 'partial rebalancing' logic for its trading signals to reduce turnover and transaction costs, and prioritize equal weighted portfolios over value weighted ones for better risk adjusted returns.
Also tests (no cards written): GPT-4 intraday news long short drift (equal weighted, 25% partial rebalancing); GPT-4 intraday news long short drift (value weighted, daily rebalancing); GPT-4 intraday news long short drift (value weighted, 50% partial rebalancing); GPT-4 intraday news long short drift (value weighted, 25% partial rebalancing); GPT-4 long only strategy (good news); GPT-4 short only strategy (bad news); GPT-4 strategy excluding small/illiquid stocks

[P155] Caught on tape: Institutional trading, stock returns, and earnings announcements (Prof Tarun Ramadorai, 2008, Oxford University Research Archive (ORA) (University of Oxford), cited by 392, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2008.03.006
Question: Do institutional trading flows inferred from transaction data predict earnings surprises and post earnings price drift?
Data: US stocks (NYSE/CRSP), 1995:Q1 to 2000:Q4, 2,153 firms, 31,114 observations, Trade and Quotes (TAQ) and Spectrum (13-F) data
Method: Infer daily institutional ownership changes from trade data using a statistical model, then regress these flows on earnings surprises and cumulative returns over 60 days after announcements
Findings:
  * Cumulative institutional flows over 60 days before earnings predict earnings surprise (coefficient 0.018, t stat 4.509, Table 9)
  * Cumulative institutional flows predict post earnings announcement drift over [+1,+60] days (coefficient 0.385, t stat 2.674, Table 10)
  * Institutional trades generate short term losses but longer term profits (Abstract)
  * Daily institutional trades are highly persistent and respond positively to recent daily returns (Abstract)
  * Extreme earnings surprise deciles show cumulative abnormal returns diverging by approximately 4-5% over 60 days (Figure 3)
Strength: strong (Large sample size (2,153 firms) and rigorous flow inference method, but sample period ends in 2000)
Limits: Sample period ends in 2000 (no evidence of current performance), requires expensive TAQ data, institutional flows are inferred not observed directly
For traders: Institutions anticipate earnings and drift; following their long term flow direction may work, but short term flows may reverse
For the app: Feature: Flag stocks with high pre earnings institutional flow to confirm earnings storylines

[P173] Stock Price Reaction to News: The Joint Effect of Tone and Attention on Momentum (Thanh Huynh, Daniel R. Smith, 2017, Journal of Behavioral Finance, cited by 29, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/15427560.2017.1339190
Question: How do the tone (positive/negative) and attention (frequency) of news items jointly affect the continuation of stock price movements (momentum) across international markets?
Data: 10.1 million news items across 4 regions (US, Europe, Japan, Asia Pacific); specific sample size of stocks and years not reported in the provided text.
Method: The study analyzes a large dataset of news items to measure news tone and attention (frequency), then tests if stocks with important and positive news show stronger return continuation (momentum) compared to others, suggesting market underreaction to good news.
Findings:
  * Stocks having important and positive news exhibit stronger return continuation.
  * The market's underreaction to good news is a driver of weekly momentum returns.
  * Investors in international markets (US, Europe, Japan, Asia Pacific) show similar underreaction to the same news characteristics.
  * News appearance frequency is used to quantify news influence on market movements.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a massive dataset of 10.1 million news items across multiple regions, but the provided text lacks specific return numbers, holding periods, and cost adjustments.)
Limits: Only the abstract and citing sentences are available; specific return percentages, exact holding periods, trading costs, and whether the strategy works after 2017 are not reported. The data is second hand for most details.
For traders: Positive news that is both important and frequent may lead to price increases that continue for weeks, but the exact profit potential and costs are unknown from this text.
For the app: The app should weight news signals by both 'tone' (positive/negative) and 'attention' (frequency/repetition) to predict which stocks are likely to drift upward after a good news event.

[P194] The Disposition Effect and Under-Reaction to News (Andrea Frazzini, 2005, unknown venue, cited by 880, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.196.9338
Question: Does investor cost basis (capital gains/losses) predict post announcement stock price drift?
Data: US stocks, 1980-2003, Mutual fund holdings data, TAQ data, I/B/E/S data
Method: Construct reference price from mutual fund holdings to measure capital gains overhang, sort stocks by overhang, trade on news events (earnings or analyst revisions)
Findings:
  * Monthly alphas of over 200 basis points (Abstract)
  * Net monthly alphas of 0.885% and 1.062% (Table VIII, 3 and 6 month holding)
  * Semiannual buy and hold returns between 1.7% and 6% (Page 2038)
  * None of the alphas of the negative overhang spread portfolios is significantly different from zero (Page 2037)
  * Overhang spread portfolio displays price drift following analysts’ recommendation changes (Page 2044)
Strength: strong (Large sample size, detailed trading cost analysis, published in top finance journal)
Limits: Data ends in 2003, mutual fund holdings data is expensive, negative overhang strategies show no profit
For traders: Focus on earnings surprises where investors have matching unrealized gains or losses
For the app: Add a 'Cost Basis Overhang' metric to news alerts

[P195] Which News Moves Stock Prices? A Textual Analysis (Jacob Boudoukh A, Ronen Feldman, Shimon Kogan et al., 2013, National Bureau of Economic Research, cited by 222, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3386/w18725
Question: Does identifying specific news events and their sentiment explain stock price movements and predict short term drift or reversal?
Data: S&P 500 stocks, Dow Jones Newswire, CRSP returns, 2000-2009, 791 companies
Method: Textual analysis to classify news days (identified vs unidentified vs no news), measure sentiment, then test return autocorrelation and zero cost trading strategies based on extreme moves and news type.
Findings:
  * Identified news days show continuation (0.7% positive autocorrelation), no news days show reversal (-3.7%).
  * No news reversal strategy earns 15.6bp per day (alpha 0.16%).
  * Identified news continuation strategy earns 19.6bp per day (alpha 0.20%).
  * Positive sentiment filter on continuation strategy increases alpha to 34bp per day.
  * Unidentified news days show no significant alpha (indistinguishable from zero).
Strength: moderate (10-year sample with daily data and clear classification rules, though transaction costs for daily trading are noted as significant.)
Limits: Sample ends 2009, daily holding period implies high costs, results may not apply to post-2010 markets.
For traders: Focus on days with clear, identified news events for momentum, avoid trading on noise or no news days where prices revert.
For the app: Classify news as "identified event" vs "noise" and flag sentiment to filter continuation signals; warn users that daily holding incurs high costs.

[P205] Daily market news sentiment and stock prices (David E. Allen, Michael J. McAleer, Abhay Kumar Singh, 2019, Applied Economics, cited by 85, read from: full text (Unpaywall repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/00036846.2018.1564115
Question: Can sentiment derived from Twitter data using natural language processing and machine learning predict next day stock returns and outperform a buy and hold strategy?
Data: 104 top NASDAQ stocks, United States, March 15, 2016 to June 15, 2016 (3 months), 676,000 tweets, data from data.world and Yahoo Finance.
Method: The author used NLP (VADER, Naive Bayes, BERT) to score tweet sentiment, then fed sentiment features into Random Forest and K Nearest Neighbor classifiers to predict if the next day's return would be negative, slightly positive, or very positive. A strategy was simulated: buy if 'Very Positive', short if 'Very Negative', and hold cash otherwise. Performance was measured against a buy and hold benchmark over the 3-month period.
Findings:
  * Using 2 features (Sentiment_Weighted, Sentiment_MA) with a 34/66 data split, K Nearest Neighbors achieved 1.29% cumulative return, while Buy and Hold lost 2.00%.
  * Using 3 features (Sentiment_Weighted, Sentiment_MA, Tweet Volume) with a 34/66 data split, K Nearest Neighbors achieved 1.374% cumulative return, while Buy and Hold lost 2.00%.
  * Using 3 features with a 66/34 data split, K Nearest Neighbors achieved 0.638% cumulative return, while Buy and Hold lost 0.636%.
  * Across both data splits, the K Nearest Neighbor classifier outperformed the Random Forest classifier in cumulative returns, with an average return of 0.915% compared to the market's average loss of 1.32%.
  * The models showed higher accuracy in detecting negative returns (down markets) than positive returns, with the 3-feature model achieving 51.0% accuracy in the 34/66 split.
Strength: weak (The study covers a very short sample period (3 months in 2016), uses a small universe of only 104 stocks, reports no transaction costs, and lacks an out of sample test period to verify if the results hold up.)
Limits: The sample is limited to 3 months in 2016; no trading costs or slippage are accounted for; the 'Buy and Hold' benchmark is negative in this specific period, making outperformance easier; the study does not test if the strategy works in different market conditions or after 2016.
For traders: While the strategy showed a profit over this specific 3-month window, the lack of cost analysis and the short timeframe mean a retail trader cannot rely on these numbers for real money; the approach is highly sensitive to the specific market environment of mid-2016.
For the app: The app should treat tweet sentiment as a short term (1-day) signal that is more reliable for identifying downside risk (shorting) than upside potential, but must warn users that this signal degrades quickly and requires real time data processing.

Themes: Text and attention signals

[P214] Feverish Stock Price Reactions to COVID-19* (Stefano Ramelli, Alexander F. Wagner, 2020, The Review of Corporate Finance Studies, cited by 1,199, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rcfs/cfaa012
Question: Do specific firm characteristics like China trade exposure, cash holdings, and leverage, or signals from conference call tone, predict stock returns during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic?
Data: US stock market (non financial and financial firms), January 2, 2020 to April 3, 2020. Sample includes firms with data on China exposure, foreign revenue, cash, and leverage. Data sources: Compustat, Hoberg and Moon (China exposure), conference call transcripts (Loughran and McDonald dictionary).
Method: The authors calculate cumulative abnormal returns (CAPM adjusted) for firms over three distinct phases of the pandemic (Incubation, Outbreak, Fever). They run regressions to see if firm characteristics (China exposure, foreign revenue, cash, leverage) and conference call tone (negativity) explain the differences in returns across firms during these periods.
Findings:
  * In the 'Outbreak' period, a one standard deviation higher exposure to China was associated with 1.36% lower cumulative returns.
  * In the 'Fever' period, a one standard deviation higher cash holding (25.80%) was associated with approximately 2.99% higher cumulative returns.
  * In the 'Fever' period, high leverage was associated with significantly lower returns (coefficient -0.135), while high cash was associated with higher returns (coefficient +0.112).
  * Firms that discussed COVID-19 on conference calls had, on average, lower cumulative returns over the whole period compared to those that did not.
  * The negative impact of leverage and positive impact of cash reversed briefly (March 23-25) after Fed intervention but resumed their original direction by April 3, 2020.
Strength: strong (The study uses a rare, exogenous shock (pandemic onset) with high frequency daily data and clear event windows, allowing for causal inference on how specific fundamentals drive returns during a crisis.)
Limits: The results are specific to the extreme volatility of the 2020 pandemic period and may not apply to normal market conditions; the study does not report transaction costs or test if these strategies work in years other than 2020.
For traders: During a sudden global health or trade crisis, investors should avoid firms with high supply chain exposure to the affected region and favor firms with strong cash reserves and low debt.
For the app: The app should flag stocks with high 'China exposure' or 'foreign revenue' as high risk during global health alerts, and prioritize 'high cash/low debt' firms as defensive holdings; it should also monitor conference call transcripts for increased negativity as a confirmation signal of distress.

[P254] In Search of Attention (Zhi Da, JOSEPH ENGELBERG, Pengjie Gao, 2011, The Journal of Finance, cited by 3,079, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2011.01679.x
Question: Does a spike in Google search volume for a stock ticker predict short term price increases followed by long term reversals, and does this apply to IPOs?
Data: US Russell 3000 stocks and IPOs; sample period January 2004 to June 2008 (non IPO) and 2004-2007 (IPOs); data source: Google Trends (SVI), CRSP, SEC Dash-5 reports.
Method: The authors calculate Abnormal Search Volume (ASVI) as the log of the current week's search volume minus the median of the previous eight weeks. They run cross sectional regressions to see if ASVI predicts abnormal returns over the next 1 to 4 weeks and weeks 5 to 52. For IPOs, they regress first day returns and long run performance (weeks 5-52) on pre IPO ASVI.
Findings:
  * An increase in ASVI predicts a positive abnormal return of 18.7 basis points in week 1 and 14.9 basis points in week 2 for Russell 3000 stocks (US, 2004-2008).
  * The predictive effect disappears by week 3 and turns negative in week 4 (-1.6 basis points), indicating a price reversal within the year.
  * For IPOs, a one standard deviation increase in pre IPO ASVI leads to a 3.18% higher first day return (US, 2004-2007).
  * IPOs with high pre IPO ASVI and high first day returns show significant long run underperformance (reversal) over the 4 to 12 months following the IPO.
  * ASVI captures retail investor attention specifically, as shown by correlations with small order sizes in SEC Dash-5 data.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large sample of 3,606 stocks over 4.5 years with a novel, direct data source (Google Trends) and robust statistical controls, though the sample ends in 2008.)
Limits: Data only covers 2004-2008, a period of high retail interest but before modern social media dominance; results are specific to US large cap stocks and IPOs; transaction costs and slippage are not calculated in the reported returns.
For traders: Retail traders should be cautious: a sudden spike in search interest often signals a short term price bump driven by emotional buying, followed by a drop as the hype fades.
For the app: Implement a 'Hype Alert' feature: flag stocks with a sharp rise in search volume (ASVI) as potential short term buys with a strict 2-week exit rule, and flag high search IPOs as potential short candidates for the 4-12 month period.

[P278] Corporate Sustainability: First Evidence on Materiality (Mozaffar Khan, George Serafeim, Aaron S. Yoon, 2016, The Accounting Review, cited by 1,935, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.2308/accr-51383
Question: Does distinguishing between material and immaterial sustainability investments predict future stock returns?
Data: US stocks, 1991 to 2012, 2,307 unique firms, 13,397 firm years, KLD and SASB data
Method: Calendar time portfolio stock return regressions using five factor models to measure alpha of portfolios sorted on material and immaterial sustainability scores
Findings:
  * Top material portfolio alpha ranges from about 3% to about 8% annualized (significant)
  * Immaterial portfolio high vs low difference is -1.49% (equal weighted) or 0.71% (value weighted), not significant
  * Material investment firms (good material, bad immaterial) alpha is 6.01%, Immaterial investment firms (bad material, good immaterial) alpha is 0.60%, difference is 5.41% annually
  * No investment firms have an estimated alpha of -2.90%
  * Firms with better material performance have more positive changes in profitability margins up to three years in the future
Strength: strong (Large sample size (13,397 firm years) and rigorous factor models distinguish material from immaterial issues clearly)
Limits: Holding period and entry timing not explicitly stated in days; transaction costs not included; data (KLD) is proprietary and paid; sample ends in 2012
For traders: Focus on sustainability news only if it relates to industry specific material issues, as immaterial spending does not drive returns
For the app: Add a filter to weight news by industry materiality (e.g., water usage matters more for beverage companies than tech firms)

[P280] Do Brokerage Analysts' Recommendations Have Investment Value? (Kent L. Womack, 1996, The Journal of Finance, cited by 1,916, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1996.tb05205.x
Question: Do stock prices continue to drift in the direction of brokerage analysts' buy and sell recommendations after the initial announcement, and if so, for how long and by how much?
Data: US stock market, 1989-1991, sample of 1,048 recommendation changes from 14 major brokerage firms using First Call data.
Method: The author tracks size adjusted stock returns for specific windows: a 3-day event window around the recommendation date, the first month after the event, and a 6-month period after the event. Returns are compared against size based benchmarks (CRSP size deciles) to isolate abnormal performance.
Findings:
  * For stocks added to buy lists, the mean size adjusted return in the first month after the event (starting 2 days post announcement) is +2.4%.
  * For stocks added to sell lists, the mean size adjusted return over the 6-month period after the event is -9.1%.
  * The total market impact (event return plus drift) for stocks added to buy lists is +5.4% over the event plus one month.
  * The total market impact for stocks added to sell lists is -13.7% over the event plus six months.
  * The market reaction to sell recommendations is significantly larger and longer lasting than for buy recommendations; buy drift is short lived (1 month) while sell drift extends for 6 months.
Strength: strong (The study uses a comprehensive, high quality dataset (First Call) with precise event dates, a large sample size, and rigorous size adjusted benchmarks over a multi year period.)
Limits: The sample period is limited to 1989-1991; the paper does not report returns after transaction costs; the 'removed from' lists have smaller sample sizes and the data does not track how long a stock stays on a list, making long term holding strategies harder to verify precisely.
For traders: Retail traders can potentially capture excess returns by buying stocks immediately after a new 'buy' rating and holding for one month, or shorting stocks after a new 'sell' rating and holding for six months, though the sell side opportunity is larger.
For the app: The app should flag 'Added to Sell' recommendations as high confidence, long duration (6-month) bearish signals, while treating 'Added to Buy' signals as short term (1-month) bullish opportunities that may fade quickly.

[P316] Firm-Level Political Risk: Measurement and Effects* (Tarek A. Hassan, Stephan Hollander, Laurence van Lent et al., 2019, The Quarterly Journal of Economics, cited by 1,481, read from: full text (Unpaywall repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjz021
Question: Does the share of time firm managers spend discussing political risks in earnings calls predict future stock returns or firm actions?
Data: US listed firms, quarterly earnings conference call transcripts, sample period not fully specified in provided text but covers years up to 2019; data source: proprietary collection of transcripts and text analysis libraries.
Method: The authors use computational linguistics to calculate a 'Political Risk' (PRisk) score for each firm quarter, defined as the weighted share of bigrams related to political topics appearing near synonyms for 'risk' or 'uncertainty' in earnings call transcripts. They validate this by checking correlations with firm actions (lobbying, hiring, investment) and stock volatility, rather than testing a specific trading strategy for returns.
Findings:
  * Firms with higher PRisk scores significantly increase lobbying and political donations in the following quarter, while non political risk measures do not predict these actions.
  * Firms with higher PRisk scores retrench (reduce) hiring and investment, indicating real economic consequences of the measured risk.
  * The measure correlates strongly (0.82) with aggregate Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) indices, validating it captures broad political uncertainty.
  * About two thirds of the variation in political risk is idiosyncratic (firm level) rather than driven by sector or aggregate economic factors.
  * The paper does not report specific stock return figures, holding periods, or trading costs for a strategy based on this signal.
Strength: strong (The study uses a novel, validated text based measure on a large sample of US firms and demonstrates strong correlations with real world firm behaviors (lobbying, investment) and volatility, though it lacks a direct trading return test.)
Limits: The provided text is an excerpt and does not contain the full sample size, specific start/end years, or any data on stock returns, holding periods, or trading costs; the paper focuses on measuring risk and its effect on real firm decisions, not on generating trading profits.
For traders: This paper confirms that political risk is a real, measurable factor that causes firms to cut investment and hire less, which may eventually hurt stock prices, but it does not provide a specific rule for when to buy or sell to profit from this.
For the app: The app should include a 'Political Risk Score' derived from earnings call transcripts as a fundamental risk metric to flag companies likely to reduce investment or face regulatory headwinds, rather than as a direct buy/sell trigger.
Themes: Text and attention signals

[P326] Input Specificity and the Propagation of Idiosyncratic Shocks in Production Networks * (Jean-Noël Barrot, Julien Sauvagnat, 2016, The Quarterly Journal of Economics, cited by 1,333, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw018
Question: Do stock prices of customer firms and related suppliers drop when a supplier is hit by a natural disaster, and does this drop depend on whether the input is specific?
Data: US public firms, 1978 to 2013, 1,082 customer firm disaster pairs and 2,004 supplier firm disaster pairs, using Compustat Segment files for links and SHELDUS for disaster data.
Method: The authors identify natural disasters hitting a supplier's headquarters county as an exogenous shock. They calculate cumulative average abnormal returns (CAAR) for customer firms and other suppliers over specific windows (e.g., 10 days before to 40 days after) using a Fama French three factor model to adjust for market risk.
Findings:
  * Customer firms experience a cumulative abnormal return (CAAR) drop of 1.13% over the 51-day window [-10, +40] when a supplier is hit by a disaster (Table IX).
  * Directly hit suppliers experience a CAAR drop of 2.46% over the same 51-day window [-10, +40] (Table IX).
  * The drop in customer stock prices is significantly larger (-2.37%) when the disrupted supplier produces specific inputs compared to non specific inputs, where the effect is statistically insignificant (0.58%) (Table X).
  * Most of the price drop for customers occurs within the first 21 days (window [-10, +10]), with a CAAR of -0.85% (sum of -0.49% and -0.36% from Table IX), suggesting rapid market reaction.
  * Related suppliers (those sharing a customer with the disrupted firm) see a 3.8 percentage point decrease in sales growth, indicating negative spillovers rather than substitution benefits (Table XI).
Strength: strong (The study uses a clean natural experiment (natural disasters) to isolate idiosyncratic shocks and employs rigorous statistical controls for cross sectional correlation in returns.)
Limits: The study relies on natural disasters which are rare events (41 major disasters in 35 years), limiting the sample size for trading strategies; it does not report trading costs or net returns after fees; the data is historical (1978-2013) and does not test performance in recent years.
For traders: This suggests that supply chain disruptions cause real value losses for customers, but the market reacts quickly (within 10-21 days), making it difficult to profit from the news unless you can identify the specific input risk before the market fully prices it in.
For the app: The app should flag customers of suppliers located in disaster prone areas if those suppliers produce 'specific' (hard to replace) inputs, and alert users that the market reaction is likely to be front loaded (happening within 2 weeks).

The app can verify the 'specificity' of the link to confirm the storyline. | retail_usable: maybe | asset_class: stocks

[P332] Ratings Changes, Ratings Levels, and the Predictive Value of Analysts’ Recommendations (Brad M. Barber, Reuven Lehavy, Brett Trueman, 2010, Financial Management, cited by 126, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1755-053x.2010.01083.x
Question: Do analyst recommendation levels and changes predict future stock returns, and does combining them improve performance?
Data: US stocks, 1986-2006, Zacks and First Call databases, over 1 million recommendations
Method: Form portfolios based on analyst ratings levels and changes, measure daily abnormal returns, control for price and earnings momentum
Findings:
  * Combined levels- and changes based hedge strategy of purchasing single upgrades to buy or strong buy and shorting single downgrades to sell or strong sell generates a significant average daily abnormal return of 5.5 basis points
  * Combined levels- and changes based strategy of purchasing double upgrades to buy or strong buy and shorting double downgrades to sell or strong sell yields a significant average daily abnormal return of 5.2 basis points
  * Levels only based hedge strategy of purchasing all buys and strong buys and shorting all sells and strong sells generates an average daily abnormal return of 3.5 basis points
  * Changes only based hedge strategy of purchasing all single upgrades and shorting all single downgrades earns an average daily abnormal return of 2.5 basis points
  * Upgrades are associated with an average daily abnormal return of 1.9 basis points versus -1.0 for downgrades
Strength: strong (Large sample size (over 1 million recommendations) and long time period (21 years) with robust controls)
Limits: Provided text omits some table details; returns are before transaction costs; sample ends in 2006 so recent performance is not tested
For traders: Combining rating levels with changes improves returns over using either alone, but costs may reduce profits
For the app: Add analyst rating changes as a trigger event and weight them by the current rating level to confirm storylines
Also tests (no cards written): Long only: Buy all Buys and Strong Buys; Long only: Buy all Upgrades; Short only: Short all Sells and Strong Sells; Short only: Short all Downgrades

[P334] The Value of Client Access to Analyst Recommendations (T. Clifton Green, 2006, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, cited by 244, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0022109000002404
Question: Does early access to analyst stock recommendations provide brokerage clients with profitable short term trading opportunities before the news becomes public?
Data: Nasdaq listed stocks, United States, 1999 through 2002, sample of 7,177 recommendation changes (2,727 upgrades, 4,450 downgrades) from 16 major brokerage firms.
Method: The study measures price changes and trading profits using intraday data with precise time stamps. It compares returns for clients who trade immediately after receiving recommendations (pre market) against transaction costs (effective bid ask spreads) and benchmarks (size/industry matching and Fama French three factor model). It also tests a calendar based strategy that rebalances daily.
Findings:
  * After controlling for transaction costs, purchasing quickly following upgrades results in an average two day return of 1.02%.
  * Selling short following downgrades produces an average two day return of 1.50%.
  * Short term profit opportunities persist for roughly two hours following the pre market release of new recommendations.
  * A calendar based strategy (buying upgrades, selling downgrades) produces positive abnormal daily returns of over 10 basis points, roughly 30% annualized.
  * Approximately one quarter of the total price impact of an upgrade occurs over the following two trading days, with the rest happening immediately or over the next month.
Strength: strong (The study uses high frequency intraday data to precisely measure entry points and transaction costs, and the results are robust across different portfolio weighting schemes and sub periods.)
Limits: The sample is limited to Nasdaq stocks from 1999-2002; the strategy relies on 'early access' (quasi private information) which is not available to the general public, and the paper does not test if this specific alpha persists in post-2002 data.
For traders: Individual traders cannot replicate these specific returns because the profit comes from acting on information before it hits the public news wires; by the time a retail trader sees the news, the price has likely already moved.
For the app: The app should flag analyst recommendation changes as high priority events but warn users that the immediate price jump often happens before public release; the app should focus on tracking the 'drift' that continues for 2 days to 1 month rather than trying to catch the initial spike.

[P337] Can Investors Profit from the Prophets? Security Analyst Recommendations and Stock Returns (Brad M. Barber, Reuven Lehavy, Maureen F. McNichols et al., 2001, The Journal of Finance, cited by 1,100, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00336
Question: Can investors profit from security analyst recommendations after accounting for trading costs?
Data: US stocks, 1986 to 1996, Zacks database (360,000 recommendations from 269 brokerage houses)
Method: Form portfolios based on consensus analyst recommendations, rebalance at different frequencies (daily, weekly, monthly), measure abnormal returns net of estimated transaction costs
Findings:
  * Most favorable stocks earn 4.13% annual abnormal gross return (1986-1996)
  * Least favorable stocks earn -4.91% annual abnormal gross return (1986-1996)
  * Daily rebalancing is crucial for positive returns on most favorable stocks
  * Transaction costs (0.727% to 4.12% round trip) eliminate abnormal net returns
  * Shorting least favorable stocks yields up to 3% annual net return but not reliably significant
Strength: strong (Large sample (360,000 recommendations), detailed cost analysis, robust to risk factors)
Limits: Sample ends in 1996; net returns not significant after costs; shorting difficult for retail
For traders: Analyst consensus changes predict drift, but trading costs wipe out profits for most strategies
For the app: Track consensus changes as events, but warn users that frequent trading costs may erase gains
Also tests (no cards written): Buy consensus 'strong buy' stocks (2-week reaction delay); Short consensus 'strong sell' stocks (2-week reaction delay); Buy consensus 'strong buy' stocks (1-month reaction delay); Short consensus 'strong sell' stocks (1-month reaction delay); Buy consensus 'strong buy' stocks (small cap subset); Short consensus 'strong sell' stocks (small cap subset); Buy consensus 'strong buy' stocks (medium cap subset); Short consensus 'strong sell' stocks (medium cap subset); Buy consensus 'strong buy' stocks (large cap subset); Short consensus 'strong sell' stocks (large cap subset)

[P354] Do Earnings Estimates Add Value to Sell-Side Analysts’ Investment Recommendations? (Ambrus Kecskés, Roni Michaely, Kent L. Womack, 2016, Management Science, cited by 67, read from: full text (Unpaywall repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2385
Question: Do stock recommendation changes by analysts that are accompanied by earnings estimate revisions lead to larger and longer lasting price movements than those without such revisions?
Data: US stock market, 1994 to 2010, sample includes all firms with analyst recommendations and earnings estimates; data sources include I/B/E/S for estimates and recommendations, CRSP for returns.
Method: The authors compare the initial price reaction and the post event drift of two groups: recommendations accompanied by earnings estimate revisions ('earnings based') versus those without ('non earnings based'). They construct trading strategies that buy upgrades and sell downgrades for both groups, holding portfolios for 1, 10, or 21 trading days, and calculate risk adjusted returns (alphas) using a four factor model.
Findings:
  * Earnings based upgrades have a 65% larger initial price reaction (+3.64% vs +2.21%) and a 166% larger one month drift (+1.62% vs +0.61%) compared to non earnings based upgrades.
  * Earnings based downgrades have a 186% larger initial price reaction (-5.06% vs -1.77%) and a 53% larger one month drift (-1.04% vs -0.68%) compared to non earnings based downgrades.
  * A trading strategy buying earnings based upgrades and selling earnings based downgrades earns a risk adjusted return (alpha) of 3.11% per month for a one month holding period.
  * The unconditional strategy (buying all upgrades and selling all downgrades regardless of earnings estimates) earns an alpha of 1.80% per month for a one month holding period.
  * The profitability of the earnings based strategy persisted throughout the 1994-2010 sample period, with similar performance at the beginning and end of the sample.
Strength: strong (The study uses a long sample period (17 years), robust risk adjustment methods, and explicitly tests for persistence over time and across different market conditions.)
Limits: The study does not report specific transaction costs or slippage assumptions, though it notes results are likely greater than institutional costs; the sample ends in 2010, so performance in the most recent decade is not directly tested in the text.
For traders: Retail traders should prioritize acting on analyst recommendation changes that are explicitly supported by changes in earnings estimates, as these signals show a stronger and more persistent price drift than recommendations based on other factors.
For the app: The app should filter analyst recommendation news to flag only those accompanied by earnings estimate revisions (up or down) and prioritize these as high confidence triggers for the 'drift' storyline, while deprioritizing recommendations without estimate changes.

[P355] Analysts’ Earnings Forecast, Recommendation,and Target Price Revisions (Ronen Feldman, Joshua Livnat, Yuan Zhang, 2012, The Journal of Portfolio Management, cited by 43, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2012.38.3.120
Question: How do immediate and delayed stock returns differ when analysts revise earnings forecasts, target prices, or recommendations, and does combining these signals improve performance?
Data: US stock market (implied by Journal of Portfolio Management and typical analyst data coverage), sample period not reported in abstract or citing notes, data source: analyst consensus data (exact provider not reported).
Method: The authors compare short term market returns around the announcement of three types of analyst revisions (earnings, target price, recommendations) and test if portfolios using all three signals together generate better future returns (drift) than portfolios using only one signal type.
Findings:
  * Revisions in earnings forecasts are positively and significantly associated with short term market returns around the revisions.
  * Short term market returns around target price revisions and recommendation changes are even stronger than those for earnings forecast revisions.
  * Portfolios using information from all three types of revisions (earnings, target price, recommendations) show superior future performance (return drift) compared to portfolios using only one type of revision.
  * Citing papers note the study uses 'short event windows' and '1-month hedge return analysis' to measure these effects.
  * Citing papers confirm that each of the three signals conveys incremental information, but target price and recommendation revisions trigger stronger investor responses than earnings estimates.
Strength: moderate (Published in a top applied finance journal with a clear comparative design, but specific return magnitudes, holding periods, and cost assumptions are missing from the available text.)
Limits: Only the abstract and citing sentences are available; exact return numbers, specific holding periods (days/weeks), transaction cost assumptions, and sample dates are not reported. The 'still works' status cannot be confirmed as no post-2012 replication data is provided in the text.
For traders: Traders should not rely on earnings surprises alone; combining them with target price and recommendation changes creates a stronger signal for short term moves and longer term drift.
For the app: The app should weight 'target price revisions' and 'recommendation changes' higher than 'earnings forecast revisions' when calculating the strength of a storyline, and flag cases where all three signals move in the same direction as high confidence events.

[P357] The Cross Section of Analyst Recommendations (Sorin M. Sorescu, Avanidhar Subrahmanyam, 2006, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, cited by 123, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0022109000002453
Question: How do analyst experience and reputation affect short- and long term stock price reactions to recommendation changes?
Data: Not reported in provided text (abstract only); sample size, country, and years not available
Method: Compare stock price reactions to analyst recommendations based on analyst attributes like experience and reputation
Findings:
  * Long term returns following recommendation changes by highly experienced analysts outperform those of low experience analysts
  * Investors appear to overreact to dramatic upgrades of low ability analysts
  * Investors appear to underreact to small upgrades by high ability analysts
  * Results are consistent with behavioral theory that agents emphasize signal strength over analyst ability
  * The study analyzes both short term and long term price reactions
Strength: moderate (Published in a peer reviewed journal with high citations, but specific return data is missing from the provided text)
Limits: Only the abstract and metadata are provided; specific return percentages, holding periods, entry points, sample years, and cost assumptions are not reported in this text
For traders: Prioritize recommendations from experienced analysts and be cautious of dramatic upgrades from less experienced ones
For the app: Filter analyst signals by experience level and magnitude of change to flag potential overreactions or underreactions in storylines

[P359] What Motivates Buy-Side Analysts to Share Recommendations Online? (Steve Crawford, Wesley R. Gray, Bryan R. Johnson et al., 2017, Management Science, cited by 35, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2017.2749
Question: Do buy side analyst recommendations posted on the SumZero social network generate significant stock returns and price drift, and which types of recommendations are most effective?
Data: US stock market (CRSP data), sample period 2008–2010, 1,751 events (recommendations posted on SumZero). Data source: SumZero platform and CRSP.
Method: The authors analyze stock returns around the dates buy side analysts posted recommendations on SumZero. They compare the performance of these stocks against benchmarks (Market Model and Factor Model) to measure abnormal returns over short and long windows. They specifically separate recommendations by direction (buy/sell) and by whether they went against the consensus of sell side analysts (contrarian).
Findings:
  * Analyst recommendations posted on SumZero generate significant returns, and prices drift in the direction of the recommendation.
  * Long window returns are particularly strong for contrarian buy recommendations.
  * Long window returns are particularly strong for most sell recommendations.
  * Analysts who share ideas are more likely to change jobs, and this likelihood is positively related to peer ratings of their recommendations.
  * Analysts with strong incentives to build a reputation (those not from top 10 universities or employed at small funds) are significantly more likely to share recommendations.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a specific, high quality dataset of professional buy side analysts (SumZero) rather than general retail sentiment, but the sample period is short (2008–2010) and relies on a single platform.)
Limits: The data is only from 2008–2010; we do not know if these returns persist today or if the platform's user base has changed. The full paper text is not available, so specific holding periods (e.g., 30 days vs 90 days) and exact return percentages are not reported. The sample is limited to US stocks.
For traders: Following buy side analysts on niche professional networks can be profitable, especially when they go against the crowd (contrarian buys) or recommend selling, but the strategy requires access to the specific platform data which may no longer be public or may have changed.
For the app: The app should prioritize ingesting data from professional only networks (if accessible) or filter for 'contrarian' signals where buy side consensus differs from sell side consensus, as these show the strongest drift.

[P413] Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors (Brad M. Barber, Terrance Odean B, 2000, The Journal of Finance, cited by 3,947, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00226
Question: Does active trading by individual investors generate returns that exceed the market after accounting for transaction costs and taxes?
Data: US stock market (NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq), 66,465 households at a large discount brokerage firm, January 1991 to December 1996. Data source: proprietary brokerage records linked to CRSP daily returns.
Method: The authors sorted households into quintiles based on trading turnover (frequency of buying and selling). They calculated gross returns (before costs) and net returns (after subtracting commissions and bid ask spreads) for each group. They compared these returns against market benchmarks (S&P 500 and value weighted indices) and adjusted for risk using the CAPM and Fama French three factor models. They also analyzed the specific timing of trades to see if bought stocks underperformed sold stocks.
Findings:
  * Most active traders (top turnover quintile) earned a net annualized geometric mean return of 11.4%, while the market returned 17.9% (US, 1991-1996).
  * Average households earned a net annual return of 16.4%, underperforming the market's 17.9% by 1.5 percentage points annually.
  * Trading costs for the average household were high: a round trip trade over $1,000 cost 3% in commissions and 1% in bid ask spread.
  * Stocks bought by individual investors underperformed the market index by 47 basis points in the month following purchase, while stocks sold outperformed the index by 2 basis points.
  * High turnover households underperformed low turnover households by 80 basis points per month (9.6% per year) based on Fama French risk adjusted returns.
Strength: strong (The study uses a unique, large scale dataset of actual household trades over six years, explicitly accounts for transaction costs, and uses robust risk adjustment models to isolate the impact of trading behavior.)
Limits: Data is from a single discount brokerage firm (1991-1996), which may not represent modern retail trading costs (which are lower) or current market conditions; the study focuses on US stocks only.
For traders: For an individual trader, the evidence suggests that frequent trading destroys wealth; holding a diversified portfolio and minimizing turnover is statistically superior to active stock picking.
For the app: The app should include a 'Trading Cost & Turnover Warning' feature that calculates the estimated drag on returns based on a user's current turnover rate and explicitly shows the performance gap between their active trades and a passive benchmark.
Themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck

[P481] Market underreaction to open market share repurchases (David L. Ikenberry, Josef Lakonishok, Theo Vermaelen, 1995, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 1,737, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405x(95)00826-z
Question: Do stock prices continue to rise for years after a company announces it is buying back its own shares on the open market, and does this effect depend on whether the stock is considered 'undervalued'?
Data: US markets (NYSE, ASE, NASD), 1980 to 1990, sample of 1,239 open market share repurchase announcements, data from CRSP and Compustat.
Method: The authors track the stock performance of companies that announced repurchases. They compare these stocks against benchmarks that match for company size and book to market ratio (a measure of value vs. glamour). They test two approaches: 1) A 'buy and hold' strategy where an investor buys the stock at the end of the announcement month and holds it for up to four years, rebalancing the portfolio annually. 2) A 'cumulative abnormal return' (CAR) calculation that measures monthly price differences against the benchmark over time.
Findings:
  * The average market reaction on the announcement day was only 3.54 percent.
  * Using a buy and hold strategy, the average excess return (above the benchmark) over four years was 12.6 percent.
  * For 'value' stocks (high book to market ratio), the average excess return over four years was 45 percent.
  * For the bottom two quintiles of stocks (low book to market), the four year excess return was close to zero or slightly negative.
  * The positive drift mostly occurred between year 1 and year 3, with returns flattening out after year 3.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large sample (1,239 firms) over an 11-year period and employs rigorous benchmarks that control for both size and value factors, which are known to influence returns.)
Limits: The data is from 1980-1990, so it is unclear if these results hold in modern markets; the study does not explicitly calculate transaction costs or taxes; the 'value' definition relies on book to market ratios which can be noisy.
For traders: An individual trader could potentially earn significant long term returns by buying stocks that announce buybacks, especially if those stocks are already considered 'cheap' or 'value' stocks, but must be prepared to hold for 3-4 years.
For the app: The app should flag companies announcing open market buybacks, specifically highlighting those with high book to market ratios, and set a 'storyline' alert to monitor the stock for a 3-4 year period to confirm the drift.

[P483] Share Issuance and Cross‐sectional Returns (Jeffrey Pontiff, Artemiza Woodgate, 2008, The Journal of Finance, cited by 638, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01335.x
Question: Does the amount of shares a company issues or repurchases over the past year or five years predict its future stock returns over periods ranging from one month to three years?
Data: US stock market (CRSP and Compustat data), 1970 to 2003 (post-1970) and 1932 to 1969 (pre-1970), 1,491,739 firm observations in the main sample.
Method: The authors use Fama Macbeth cross sectional regressions to test if the change in the number of shares outstanding (annual and 5-year measures) predicts future stock returns, controlling for size, book to market, and momentum. They test holding periods of 1 month, 6 months, and 1, 2, and 3 years.
Findings:
  * Post-1970, a one standard deviation increase in annual share issuance is associated with a 0.33% decrease in the monthly cross sectional return (slope -2.23, t stat -7.08).
  * Post-1970, a one standard deviation increase in 5-year share issuance is associated with a 0.23% decrease in the monthly cross sectional return (slope -0.71).
  * The predictive power of annual share issuance is statistically stronger than size, book to market, and momentum for all holding periods from 1 month to 3 years.
  * Pre-1970, annual share issuance was only statistically significant in 1 out of 40 specifications, and 5-year issuance was insignificant for most holding periods, suggesting the effect is specific to the post-1970 era.
  * The negative return effect persists even when removing firms that had seasoned equity offerings (SEOs), share repurchases, or stock mergers in the recent past, indicating a broader 'issuance effect'.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (over 1.4 million observations), robust statistical method (Fama Macbeth) that addresses long run return specification issues, and extensive out of sample testing across different time periods and event exclusions.)
Limits: The effect is not present in the pre-1970 data, suggesting it may be driven by changes in market structure or transaction costs after 1970; the study reports raw cross sectional regression coefficients, not explicit net returns after trading costs for a specific strategy; data on share counts is available, but the specific 'issuance' signal requires historical share count data which may be harder to reconstruct for a retail app than simple price data.
For traders: Retail traders should be cautious about buying stocks that have recently increased their share count significantly, as these stocks tend to underperform the market for up to three years; conversely, stocks with share reductions (buybacks) tend to outperform.
For the app: Add a 'Share Issuance Trend' metric to the app that flags companies with a significant increase in shares outstanding over the last 12 months or 5 years as a negative signal in the storyline, warning users that historical data suggests these stocks drift downward.

[P488] The Timing and Source of Long-Run Returns Following Repurchases (Leonce L. Bargeron, Alice A. Bonaimé, Shawn Thomas, 2017, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, cited by 48, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0022109017000084
Question: What is the timing and source of long run returns following open market share repurchase authorizations?
Data: US, 1979-2010, 18,293 authorizations, CRSP/Compustat
Method: Calendar time portfolio regressions using Fama French 3-factor model to measure monthly abnormal returns over 12 to 48 months.
Findings:
  * Returns between program authorization and completion announcements are indistinguishable from 0.
  * Postcompletion period monthly alphas: 0.6682% (12 months) to 0.2849% (48 months).
  * Full sample monthly alphas: 0.2082% (12 months) to 0.1465% (48 months).
  * Subsequent repurchase authorizations drive returns: 0.2886% (12 months) to 0.4054% (48 months).
  * Firms with no subsequent events show insignificant returns after 24 months (0.0928% to -0.0406%).
Strength: strong (Large sample of 18,293 authorizations over 30 years with rigorous calendar time regression tests.)
Limits: Data ends 2010, costs not reported, requires tracking specific events.
For traders: Do not expect drift immediately after authorization; wait for completion or subsequent events to confirm the move.
For the app: Track completion dates and flag subsequent authorization or takeover news as confirmation signals.

[P495] Asymmetric Information, Financial Reporting, and Open-Market Share Repurchases (Matthew T. Billett, Miaomiao Yu, 2016, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, cited by 54, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0022109016000612
Question: How do open market share repurchase announcements affect stock prices differently for companies with low quality financial reporting (opaque) versus high quality reporting (transparent), and do these price differences persist over time?
Data: US stock market (implied by Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis and typical sample for this topic), sample period not explicitly stated in abstract or citing sentences, data source: financial reporting quality metrics (accruals) and stock returns.
Method: The authors classify firms as 'opaque' or 'transparent' based on the quality of their financial reporting (specifically accruals quality). They then compare the stock price reactions (abnormal returns) immediately following a share repurchase announcement and the long term stock performance for these two groups, controlling for other factors like governance and earnings management.
Findings:
  * Opaque firms experience positive abnormal returns of twice the magnitude of those of transparent firms around the repurchase announcement.
  * Significant positive long run post announcement returns are documented for opaque firms.
  * No significant long run post announcement returns are documented for transparent firms.
  * Takeover activity and premiums rise with repurchase activity by opaque firms, which may explain some of the wealth effects.
  * Asymmetric information plays an important role in the wealth effects around open market share repurchases.
Strength: moderate (The study controls for governance and earnings management, but the exact sample size, specific years, and magnitude of returns are not provided in the available text.)
Limits: Only the abstract and citing sentences are available; specific sample years, exact return percentages, and holding periods are not reported. The data is second hand regarding the specific numbers, as the full text is not provided.
For traders: Retail traders might find better short term and long term gains by focusing on share repurchase announcements from companies with lower financial reporting transparency, as the market appears to underreact more significantly to these signals compared to transparent firms.
For the app: Add a 'Reporting Quality' filter to repurchase alerts: flag repurchase announcements from 'opaque' firms (high accrual variation) as high potential storylines for a drift strategy, while deprioritizing similar announcements from 'transparent' firms.

[P507] The long-run performance of stock returns following debt offerings (D. Katherine Spiess, J. F. Affleck‐Graves, 1999, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 398, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0304-405x(99)00031-8
Question: How much of the negative signal from a company issuing debt is priced in immediately versus unfolding over years, and which types of firms or market conditions make this underreaction worse?
Data: US stock market, 1975 to 1989 for issuance events, with performance tracked through 1994; sample drawn from Investment Dealers' Digest Directory of Corporate Financing; data source is paid directory and CRSP return data (implied by standard practice of the era).
Method: The authors identify firms issuing straight or convertible debt, then compare their long term stock returns against a control group of non issuing firms matched by size and book to market ratio. They test if returns are lower for issuers, especially in specific subgroups (small, young, NASDAQ, speculative grade) and during years with many debt issues.
Findings:
  * Median seasoned debt issuing firms underperformed matched control firms by 18.7% over the post issue period (cited in 2000 paper).
  * Underperformance is more severe for smaller, younger, and NASDAQ listed firms, and for firms issuing speculative grade debt.
  * Underperformance is limited to periods with a high volume of debt issues; it does not appear in low volume periods.
  * Contrary to earlier studies, the market underreacts at the announcement, meaning the full negative impact is realized over the long run, not on day one.
  * Mean abnormal performance following debt issues is statistically insignificant, but the median performance is significantly negative, indicating a few large failures drive the result.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a long sample period (15 years) and a robust matching methodology (size and book to market), but the results are heavily skewed by the median (not the mean) and rely on data from a specific historical era (1975-1989) before modern market structures.)
Limits: Data is from 1975-1989 (pre-1990s); results are based on median returns which can hide average outcomes; the study relies on second hand citations for specific return numbers as the full text is not provided; it does not account for transaction costs or short selling constraints.
For traders: If a company issues debt, especially if it is small, young, or speculative, do not expect the stock to drop immediately; instead, expect a slow decline over the next 3-5 years, particularly if the market is currently flooded with new debt issues.
For the app: Add a 'Debt Issuance Watchlist' feature: when a company announces a debt offering, flag it as a 'slow burn sell' signal for a 3-5 year horizon, with higher severity scores if the firm is small, young, or has low credit ratings, and if the current month's total debt issuance volume is above the historical median.

[P517] Underperformance in long-run stock returns following seasoned equity offerings (D. Katherine Spiess, J. F. Affleck‐Graves, 1995, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 1,005, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405x(94)00817-k
Question: Do firms that issue additional shares (seasoned equity offerings) underperform similar non issuing firms in the long run?
Data: US stock market, 1975–1989, firms making seasoned equity offerings (SEO) matched by industry and size to non issuing firms.
Method: Compare the long term buy and hold returns of issuing firms against a control group of non issuing firms matched by industry and size, controlling for offer size, firm age, and book to market ratio.
Findings:
  * Firms making seasoned equity offerings substantially underperformed matched non issuing firms during 1975–1989.
  * The underperformance persists after controlling for trading system, offer size, firm age, and book to market ratio.
  * A citing paper (Predicting Secondary Equity Offerings Using Machine Learning, 2018) reports that issuing firms underperform by 31.2% over a five year horizon compared to matched firms.
  * Another citing paper (Bank regulation, financial crisis, and the announcement effects of seasoned equity offerings of US commercial banks, 2016) states equity issuers have 7% lower annual returns for the five years following each SEO.
  * The underperformance is similar to that previously documented for initial public offerings (IPOs).
Strength: moderate (Large sample size and robust matching methodology (industry and size), but the data is limited to the 1975–1989 period and relies on second hand reporting for specific return magnitudes in later citations.)
Limits: The primary text is an abstract; specific return numbers (like 31.2% or 7%) come from citing papers and may refer to slightly different samples or methodologies. The study period ends in 1989, so it does not cover modern market structures or post-2010 data.
For traders: Avoid buying stocks immediately after they announce a seasoned equity offering, as they tend to lose value relative to the market for several years.
For the app: Add a 'Seasoned Equity Offering' event trigger that flags a stock for a 'sell' or 'avoid' signal for the next 3–5 years, linking the news of the share sale to a predicted long term underperformance storyline.

[P577] An Examination of Long‐Term Abnormal Stock Returns and Operating Performance Following R&D Increases (Allan C. Eberhart, William F. Maxwell, Akhtar R. Siddique, 2004, The Journal of Finance, cited by 916, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00644.x
Question: Do stock prices drift upward for years after firms unexpectedly increase their research and development spending?
Data: US stock market (NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ), 1951 to 2001 (full sample) and 1974 to 2001 (subsample), 8,313 cases of unexpected R&D increases across 3,099 firms, data from COMPUSTAT and CRSP.
Method: The authors identify firms that unexpectedly and significantly increase R&D spending. They track these firms' stock returns over a 5-year period following the increase, comparing them to matched firms and using multi factor models (Fama French and Carhart) to calculate abnormal returns (returns above what risk models predict).
Findings:
  * Firms that unexpectedly increase R&D experience significantly positive abnormal stock returns for 5 years following the increase.
  * In the 1974 to 2001 period, value weighted abnormal returns were at least 25.2 basis points per month (approx. 3% per year) using the Carhart four factor model.
  * Equal weighted abnormal returns were higher, reaching up to 56 basis points per month (approx. 6.7% per year) in the 1974 to 2001 period.
  * High tech firms showed significantly higher abnormal returns than low tech firms, but low tech firms also showed positive (though smaller) abnormal returns.
  * Operating performance (profit margins) also improved significantly for these firms over the same 5-year period, confirming the investment was beneficial.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (8,000+ cases), long time horizon (50 years), robustness checks across different risk models and matching methods, and confirmation via operating performance data.)
Limits: The study relies on accounting data (COMPUSTAT) which has survivorship bias (though they tested for this); the signal is based on historical accounting ratios, not real time news; the sample ends in 2001, so recent performance is not tested; transaction costs are not explicitly calculated in the paper.
For traders: An individual trader could potentially profit by buying stocks that unexpectedly raise R&D spending and holding them for several years, as the market tends to underreact to the long term value of these investments.
For the app: The app should scan annual or quarterly filings to detect when a company's R&D to sales ratio jumps significantly compared to its own history, flag these as 'long term growth story' candidates, and alert the user to hold for 3-5 years rather than selling on short term volatility.

SurpriseRD is 0 otherwise. | direction: both (buy the top group, sell short the bottom group) | entry: portfolio formed at the start of the month after the signal is known, rebalanced in month 6 | holding_days: about 21 (1 month) | reported_return: 0.29% a month, long short portfolio, t stat 3.54 (as reported in the original paper) | after_costs: no (returns before trading costs) | stocks: US stocks (CRSP), equal weighted | market_years: US, 1974 to 2001 | still_works: not reported (monthly returns not loaded) | data_needed: company accounts: paid as a database (Compustat), free from SEC filings by hand | storyline_fit: not reported (dataset) | retail_usable: not reported (dataset) | asset_class: stocks | source: Open Source Asset Pricing, signal SurpriseRD: fields method, trigger, direction, entry, holding_days, reported_return, after_costs, stocks, market_years, still_works, data_needed come from the dataset

[P599] The Long-Term Effects of Hedge Fund Activism (Lucian A. Bebchuk, Alon P. Brav, Wei Jiang, 2015, National Bureau of Economic Research, cited by 416, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3386/w21227
Question: Do stocks targeted by hedge fund activists, or stocks after activists leave, show abnormal price drift over multi year periods?
Data: US stock market, 1994 to 2014 (implied by sample start 1994 and 5-year windows), sample of 1,605+ targeted firms and 952 firms with identified exits, data from SEC filings (13D) and CRSP/Compustat.
Method: The authors identify firms targeted by activist hedge funds and track their stock performance for 3 and 5 years after the intervention. They also track performance for 3 years after the activist exits. They compare these returns to benchmark portfolios matched by size and book to market value, and run calendar time regressions to calculate abnormal returns (alpha).
Findings:
  * Value weighted buy and hold abnormal returns were positive at 2.58% over 36 months and 5.81% over 60 months, but these were not statistically significant.
  * Equal weighted buy and hold abnormal returns were 7.17% over 36 months but dropped to -0.29% over 60 months, with neither being statistically significant.
  * After an activist exits, equal weighted buy and hold abnormal returns were 19.06% over 36 months, and value weighted were 14.90%, but the paper notes these are not statistically significant in the main text despite positive alphas in regression tables.
  * Calendar time portfolio regressions show a monthly alpha of 0.37% (equal weight) and 0.31% (value weight) for the 3-year period after activist exit, which are statistically significant at 5% and 10% levels respectively.
  * The study finds no evidence of 'pump and dump' patterns where prices fall after the activist leaves; instead, returns remain positive or flat.
Strength: strong (Large sample size spanning 20 years, multiple robustness checks (firm level, portfolio, calendar time), and use of standard academic benchmarks (Fama French Carhart).)
Limits: The paper focuses on US stocks only; long horizon abnormal return tests often have low statistical power; transaction costs and liquidity constraints for small cap targets are not explicitly modeled in the return figures.
For traders: An individual trader might find a slight edge in buying stocks after an activist exits, but the edge is small, requires a 3-year hold, and may disappear after accounting for trading costs and the difficulty of identifying exits early.
For the app: Add a 'Post Activist Exit' storyline tracker that flags companies where an activist has recently sold their stake, warning users that a 3-year drift might occur but emphasizing the long holding period required.

[P615] Anomalies and Market Efficiency (G. William Schwert, 2002, National Bureau of Economic Research, cited by 547, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3386/w9277
Question: Do well known stock market anomalies persist after publication, and do they survive trading costs and recent market conditions?
Data: US stocks (NYSE, Amex, Nasdaq), sample periods ranging from 1885 to 2002, data from CRSP, S&P, and DFA funds
Method: Review of academic literature and replication of anomaly tests using portfolio regression analysis (CAPM and Fama French three factor model) to measure abnormal returns (alpha) over different time periods
Findings:
  * Size effect alpha 0.2% per month (1982-2002), t stat 0.67 (not reliable)
  * Value effect (B/M) alpha -0.2% per month (1994-2002), t stat -0.59 (not reliable)
  * Momentum effect alpha 1% per month (1990-2001), t stat 2.7 to 7.0 (reliable)
  * Weekend effect disappeared since 1978 (alpha not reliably different from zero)
  * IPO stocks yield below normal returns in 36 months following IPO (Ritter 1991)
Strength: moderate (Large sample size and long history (1885-2002), but some tables and details omitted in provided text)
Limits: Many tables and specific return details omitted in provided text ('[... part of the paper left out ...]'); transaction costs not quantified in results
For traders: Many anomalies vanish after publication; momentum persists; transaction costs are critical for economic significance
For the app: Prioritize momentum and event driven underperformance (IPO); avoid static size/value rules as they likely disappeared
Also tests (no cards written): M&A Bidder Long Run Underperformance; Interest Rate Predictability; Inflation Predictability
