[P4259] Do Investors Trade Too Much? (Terrance Odean B, 1999, American Economic Review, cited by 2,244, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.89.5.1279
Question: Do retail investors trade too much and lose money on their trades compared to holding?
Data: US discount brokerage accounts, 1987-1993, ~50,000 transactions, CRSP daily return files
Method: Compare returns of securities bought versus securities sold by the same investors over 4 months, 1 year, and 2 years, adjusting for costs and risk factors
Findings:
  * Securities bought underperform securities sold by 1.36% over 84 trading days (Panel A)
  * Securities bought underperform securities sold by 3.31% over 252 trading days (Panel A)
  * Average total cost of a round trip trade is about 5.9 percent (commission plus spread)
  * Calendar time portfolios show monthly excess returns of -0.293% for 4-month formation periods (Table 2)
  * Even when controlling for size and book to market, purchases underperform sales (Table 3)
Strength: strong (Uses actual brokerage data with precise cost tracking and bootstrapping for significance across multiple horizons)
Limits: Data is from 1987-1993 when costs were high; does not test performance after publication; costs may be lower today
For traders: Retail investors tend to sell winners and buy losers, resulting in underperformance after costs; avoid chasing recent winners
For the app: Flag when a user's trade mirrors the average retail investor behavior (buying recent winners) and warn about expected underperformance
Also tests (no cards written): Calendar time portfolio: Long securities bought vs. Short securities sold (24-month formation); Buy previous winners vs. Sell previous winners; Buy previous losers vs. Sell previous losers

[P4260] Just How Much Do Individual Investors Lose By Trading? (Brad M. Barber, Yi‐Tsung Lee, Yu‐Jane Liu et al., 2005, SSRN Electronic Journal, cited by 248, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.529062
Question: How much do individual investors lose from trading compared to institutions, and what are the primary drivers of these losses?
Data: Taiwan Stock Exchange (TSE), 1995–1999, complete transaction history of all traders (individuals, corporations, dealers, foreigners, mutual funds), sample includes ~2,000 traders and ~240,000 trades annually.
Method: The authors constructed portfolios mimicking the buy and sell decisions of different investor groups to measure performance. They separated trades into 'aggressive' (market orders) and 'passive' (limit orders) to attribute losses. They calculated abnormal returns using the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and the four factor model, accounting for commissions, transaction taxes, and market timing losses over horizons up to one year.
Findings:
  * Individual investor portfolios suffered an annual performance penalty of 3.8 percentage points (Taiwan, 1995–1999).
  * Institutional investors enjoyed an annual performance boost of 1.5 percentage points after commissions and taxes (Taiwan, 1995–1999).
  * Virtually all individual trading losses are traced to their aggressive orders, while both aggressive and passive institutional trades are profitable.
  * Total losses for individual investors from 1995 to 1999 were $NT 935 billion, equivalent to 2.2% of Taiwan's GDP or 2.8% of total personal income.
  * Most losses and gains accrue within a few weeks of the trade and reach an asymptote at a horizon of six months.
Strength: strong (The study uses a unique, complete dataset of every trade in a major market, allowing for precise attribution of losses to specific trader types and order types without sampling bias.)
Limits: Data is from Taiwan (1995–1999), a market with exceptionally high turnover (300% annually) and specific tax structures (0.3% transaction tax); results may not directly translate to lower turnover markets like the US or Europe, and the sample predates modern low cost commission structures.
For traders: Active trading by individuals systematically destroys wealth compared to a buy and hold strategy, primarily due to high turnover and aggressive order execution costs.
For the app: The app should include a 'Cost of Trading' calculator that estimates the drag on returns based on a user's current turnover rate and order aggressiveness, warning them if their projected costs exceed the 3.8% annual penalty observed in the study.
Themes: From signal to trade

[P4265] Do Individual Investors Ignore Transaction Costs? (Deniz Anginer, Snow Xue Han, Çelim Yıldızhan, 2025, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, cited by 0, read from: abstract only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0022109025101695
Question: Do individual investors adjust their holding periods and stock liquidity choices based on transaction costs?
Data: US (66,000 households, ~800,000 transactions) and Finland (303,000 households, ~2,000,000 transactions); specific years not reported in abstract; data source is brokerage records.
Method: The authors analyze the relationship between how long investors hold stocks and the liquidity (ease of trading) of those stocks, using large datasets of actual household transactions. They also look at how holding periods change when stock liquidity is suddenly altered by external events.
Findings:
  * Individual investors with longer holding periods tend to hold less liquid stocks (US and Finland data).
  * The link between holding periods and transaction costs is stronger for financially sophisticated households.
  * Findings are confirmed by analyzing changes around exogenous shocks to stock liquidity.
  * Individual investors do not ignore non salient costs like transaction fees; they are aware of trading costs.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a very large sample size of real transaction data from two countries, but the abstract lacks specific return figures, holding period lengths, or cost assumptions.)
Limits: Only the abstract is available; specific holding period durations, exact return numbers, trading cost assumptions, and sample years are not reported. The study describes investor behavior rather than testing a specific trading strategy for profit.
For traders: Retail traders who hold stocks for long periods may be unintentionally exposed to higher trading costs by choosing illiquid stocks, while sophisticated traders seem to manage this trade off better.
For the app: Add a warning metric that flags when a user's portfolio holds illiquid stocks for long periods, suggesting they may be paying hidden costs that erode returns.
Themes: From signal to trade

[P4266] Investor Overconfidence and Trading Volume (Meir Statman, Steven R. Thorley, Keith Vorkink, 2006, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 974, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhj032
Question: Does investor overconfidence, driven by past returns, explain high trading volume, and how does this relationship vary by stock size and time period?
Data: US market (NYSE/AMEX), August 1962 to December 2002, ~1.88 million individual stock observations (1878 securities with 10+ years of data), source: CRSP monthly and daily files.
Method: The authors use Vector Autoregressions (VAR) and impulse response functions on monthly time series data to test if past market and individual stock returns predict future trading volume (turnover), controlling for volatility and return dispersion.
Findings:
  * Market wide turnover is positively related to lagged market returns for many months; a 7% market return versus -5% leads to an 'extra month' of volume spread over the next six months.
  * Individual security turnover is positively related to both lagged security returns (disposition effect) and lagged market returns (overconfidence), with market shocks having a larger impact than security specific shocks.
  * The relationship between past returns and trading volume is more pronounced in small cap stocks and in earlier periods (1963–1982) where individual investors held a greater proportion of shares.
  * In the most recent subperiod (1993–2002), the evidence for the disposition effect (selling winners, holding losers) largely disappears, and the sensitivity of volume to market returns is weaker compared to earlier decades.
  * The lead lag relationship between returns and volume is statistically significant at the 0.01 level for the first six months following a market return shock in the full sample.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (over 1.8 million observations) spanning 40 years with robust statistical controls (VAR, impulse response) and sensitivity analysis across decades and market caps.)
Limits: The study measures aggregate market behavior and volume relationships, not specific trading strategies or returns; it does not report net returns after transaction costs, nor does it test if following these volume signals generates profit.
For traders: Individual investors should be aware that their own trading activity likely increases after market gains due to overconfidence, potentially leading to excessive trading and lower returns, especially in small cap stocks.
For the app: Add a 'Sentiment/Overconfidence' metric that flags when a user's portfolio or the broader market has had strong recent gains, warning that trading volume may be driven by emotion rather than new information.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P4269] Tax-Motivated Trading by Individual Investors (Zoran Ivkovich, James M. Poterba, Scott J. Weisbenner, 2004, National Bureau of Economic Research, cited by 59, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3386/w10275
Question: How tax incentives affect individual investors' realization of capital gains and losses
Data: US, 1991 to 1996, 23,877 households, 414,047 purchases, discount broker data
Method: Compare taxable and tax deferred accounts to identify tax motivated trading using hazard models for sale probability
Findings:
  * Hazard rate for stock sale drops from fifteen percent in the first month to less than five percent per month after six months
  * By one year after purchase, probability stock has been sold is more than 50 percent if gain, 44 percent if loss
  * Expected holding period for stock in taxable account at time of purchase is just over six years
  * Expected holding period rises to just under 14 years after a stock has been held for a year
  * Chance stock will be repurchased within 30 days if sold at loss in December is substantially lower than other months
Strength: strong (Large sample of direct trade data, but sample period ends in 1996)
Limits: Data ends 1996, US only, discount broker sample, does not test profitability of trading on these signals
For traders: Individual investors defer gains and sell losses in December, creating price pressure, but the paper does not quantify returns from trading these patterns.
For the app: Feature: flag stocks with losses in December for potential selling pressure; warning: lock in may reduce selling pressure on winners over time

[P4286] Portfolio Concentration and the Performance of Individual Investors (Zoran Ivković, Clemens Sialm, Scott J. Weisbenner, 2008, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, cited by 362, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0022109000004233
Question: Do individual investors with concentrated portfolios outperform those with diversified portfolios, and is this due to skill or luck?
Data: US discount broker data, 1991 to 1996, 640,070 buy transactions and 552,832 sell transactions
Method: Compare stock trade performance and portfolio holdings between households with concentrated portfolios (few stocks) and diversified portfolios (many stocks) using regression and portfolio analysis
Findings:
  * Stocks purchased by all households have an average excess return of –1.6 percent during the year following the purchase, while stocks sold have 0.2 percent
  * Trades of concentrated investors outperform those made by diversified investors by 0.8 percentage points on an annual basis (all households)
  * For households with portfolios of at least $100,000, concentrated trades outperform diversified trades by 3.3 percentage points per year (excess return)
  * Intersection of non S&P 500 and local stocks yields 59 basis points per month (7.3 percentage points annualized) for all households
  * Holdings of concentrated investors outperform diversified holdings by 16 basis points per month (1.9 percentage points annualized)
Strength: strong (Large sample size of over 1 million transactions with robustness tests across concentration measures and horizons)
Limits: Data ends in 1996, US discount broker only, transaction costs not explicitly deducted, concentration data not public
For traders: Concentration can signal superior stock picking skill but increases total risk and lowers Sharpe ratios compared to diversification
For the app: Flag when a tracked investor concentrates on a stock with a developing news storyline as a potential skill signal

[P4288] Talk and Action: What Individual Investors Say and What They Do (Daniel Dorn, Gur Huberman, 2005, European Finance Review, cited by 424, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10679-005-4997-z
Question: Do individual investors' self reported psychological traits (like risk aversion or overconfidence) explain their actual trading behavior and portfolio choices better than objective traits like age or gender?
Data: German retail brokerage clients, 1995 to May 2000, 21,500 potential participants with transaction records, 1,345 survey respondents. Data source: Brokerage transaction logs and a paper/online survey.
Method: The authors matched daily trading records with survey responses to regress actual portfolio behavior (diversification and turnover) against both objective attributes (age, gender, income) and subjective attributes (self reported risk aversion, perceived knowledge, illusion of control).
Findings:
  * Self reported risk aversion is the single most important determinant of both portfolio diversification and trading turnover.
  * Investors who report being more risk tolerant hold less diversified portfolios and trade more aggressively.
  * Less experienced investors tend to churn poorly diversified portfolios; a one standard deviation increase in experience is associated with a decrease in monthly turnover from 9.5% to 8%.
  * Investors who think they are more knowledgeable than the average investor churn their portfolios more, even if they hold better diversified portfolios.
  * The most aggressive traders earn significantly lower portfolio returns than the least aggressive traders, but their performance is similar before transaction costs, indicating trading costs are the primary cause of underperformance.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a unique dataset linking actual trades with self reported psychology, but the sample is limited to one German broker and the analysis is cross sectional rather than a test of a trading strategy.)
Limits: The sample is from a single German discount broker between 1995 and 2000; the paper does not propose a trading strategy, report specific abnormal returns for a signal, or test if the findings hold in other markets or recent years.
For traders: Individual investors should recognize that their own self perceived risk tolerance and overconfidence are likely driving them to trade too frequently and hold too few stocks, which destroys value through costs rather than skill.
For the app: The app should include a 'behavioral check' feature that asks users to rate their risk tolerance and confidence before executing a trade, warning them if their stated profile suggests they are overtrading or under diversifying based on the patterns found in this study.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P4363] Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses? (Terrance Odean B, 1998, The Journal of Finance, cited by 3,717, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072
Question: Do individual investors systematically sell winning stocks too soon and hold losing stocks too long, and does this behavior hurt their future returns?
Data: US stock market, 10,000 accounts at a large discount brokerage, trading records from 1987 to 1993, sample includes realized and paper (unrealized) gains and losses.
Method: The author compares the proportion of gains realized (PGR) to the proportion of losses realized (PLR) across different time periods and price ranges. He also tracks the future performance of stocks that were sold for a profit versus stocks that were held despite being at a loss (paper losses) over 84, 252, and 504 trading days.
Findings:
  * Investors realized 20.1% of gains but only 12.6% of losses in the 1987–1990 period (t statistic -23.0), showing a strong preference for selling winners.
  * In December, the pattern reverses slightly due to tax motives: 12.9% of gains were realized versus 14.3% of losses (t statistic 1.9), but the effect is weaker than the annual average.
  * Over the next 252 trading days (one year), stocks sold for a profit outperformed the market by 2.35%, while stocks held at a loss underperformed the market by 1.06%.
  * The difference in excess returns between sold winners and held losers is 3.41% over one year, with a p value of 0.001, indicating the mistake is statistically significant.
  * A hypothetical investor who sold a winner instead of a loser would lose an estimated 4.4% in value over the next year due to missed gains and lost tax benefits.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large, real world dataset of 10,000 individual accounts with full trade history, allowing for precise calculation of realized vs. unrealized gains and robust statistical testing of future performance.)
Limits: Data is from 1987–1993 (pre internet trading boom), focuses only on US discount brokerage accounts, and does not test if the strategy works after the paper was published.
For traders: Individual traders should be aware that their instinct to cut winners and hold losers is likely hurting their returns; selling losers and holding winners (for tax and performance reasons) is the mathematically superior approach.
For the app: The app should flag positions that are currently at a loss and have been held for a long time, warning the user that historical evidence suggests these stocks are likely to underperform the market if held further.
Themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck

[P4368] The Long‐Run Performance of initial Public Offerings (Jay R. Ritter, 1991, The Journal of Finance, cited by 3,499, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1991.tb03743.x
Question: What does the evidence say about the long run returns of buying or shorting IPOs after their first day of trading, and how do different benchmarks affect these results?
Data: US stocks (NYSE, Amex, NASDAQ), 1,526 IPOs issued between 1975 and 1984, sample size 1,526 IPOs and 1,526 matching firms, data source CRSP daily returns tapes.
Method: The study compares the 3-year buy and hold returns of IPOs (starting from the first closing price) against a control group of firms matched by industry and size. It also calculates cumulative average adjusted returns (CAR) using monthly rebalancing against four different benchmarks: a matching firm, the smallest size decile of the NYSE, the value weighted NASDAQ index, and the value weighted Amex NYSE index.
Findings:
  * IPOs had an average 3-year holding period return of 34.47% (exclusive of the initial first day gain), while matching firms returned 61.86% over the same period.
  * By the end of 36 months, the cumulative average matching firm adjusted return for IPOs was -29.13% (t statistic -5.89).
  * The median 3-year return for IPOs was -16.67%, compared to +38.54% for matching firms.
  * IPOs issued in high volume years (like 1983) performed the worst, with the underperformance concentrated in young growth companies.
  * Even though IPOs had higher average betas (1.39 in the first year) than matching firms (1.14), the underperformance remained significant, suggesting risk adjustment alone does not explain the result.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (1,526 IPOs), rigorous matching methodology by size and industry, and use of multiple benchmark adjustments over a full 3-year period.)
Limits: Data is limited to the 1975-1984 period; the study does not report trading costs or transaction fees; results may not apply to modern markets or different regulatory environments; the 'hot issue' market conditions of the 1980s may differ from today.
For traders: Avoid holding IPOs for the long term (3+ years) as they historically underperform similar sized companies, but the strategy of shorting them is difficult for retail traders due to borrowing costs and the risk of short squeezes in the early days.
For the app: Add a 'Long Run IPO Warning' feature: if a stock is in its first 3 years post IPO, flag it as historically likely to underperform its sector peers, and suggest reducing position size or avoiding new entries after the initial hype.

[P4539] Bayesian Kelly criterion as an allocation strategy in Finnish stock markets (Risto K. Heikkinen, 2020, Jyväskylä University Digital Archive (University of Jyväskylä), cited by 0, read from: abstract only)
Link: http://urn.fi/URN:NBN:fi:jyu-202011186677
Question: How does a Bayesian Kelly criterion allocation strategy perform on Finnish stock markets compared to traditional portfolio theory and a fixed 50% stock allocation when using analyst target prices for single stocks?
Data: Finnish stock market, 2010-2019, sample includes market index, risk free rate, and individual stocks; data source includes analyst target prices and historical returns.
Method: The study combines Bayesian modeling for return uncertainty and a safety constraint for short term risk to create an allocation algorithm. It tests two versions: one allocating wealth between a market index and risk free assets, and another adding a single stock based on analyst target prices. Performance is measured by the Sharpe ratio (risk adjusted return) and compared against traditional portfolio theory, a fixed 50% stock strategy, and the performance of Solidium (a Finnish state investment company).
Findings:
  * Bayes Kelly strategies produced better risk adjusted returns than all comparison methods based on the Sharpe ratio (Finnish market, 2010-2019).
  * Solidium's capital development nearly matched the Bayes Kelly strategy with a 20% acceptable annual loss limit, but Solidium lost the Sharpe ratio comparison due to higher return volatility.
  * Adding the most promising single stock to the portfolio based on analyst target prices did not significantly affect final wealth.
  * Adding the single stock reduced return volatility and slightly improved the Sharpe ratio.
  * The study found no clear consensus on the fixed constant for risk allocation in previous literature, which this paper addresses by combining multiple extensions.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a 10-year sample period and compares against real world benchmarks like Solidium, but relies solely on an abstract with no full text to verify cost assumptions or specific entry/exit rules.)
Limits: Only the abstract is available; specific entry timing, holding periods, transaction costs, and the exact definition of the 'safety constraint' are not reported. The results are specific to the Finnish market and the 2010-2019 period.
For traders: This suggests that dynamic allocation rules based on risk tolerance (like the 20% loss limit) can outperform static 50/50 splits, but adding single stocks based solely on analyst price targets may not significantly boost returns.
For the app: Implement a dynamic position sizing feature that adjusts exposure based on a user defined maximum acceptable loss (e.g., 20%) rather than fixed weights, and warn users that adding single stocks based on analyst targets may only reduce volatility without increasing returns.

[P4542] Practical Implementation of the Kelly Criterion: Optimal Growth Rate, Number of Trades, and Rebalancing Frequency for Equity Portfolios (Andrea Carta, Claudio Conversano, 2020, Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics, cited by 13, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fams.2020.577050
Question: How does the Kelly criterion for portfolio sizing compare to Markowitz and other strategies in terms of growth and risk?
Data: EuroStoxx50 equities (42 stocks), 2007-2018 (out of sample rolling), Banca Intesa single equity (daily data), Monte Carlo simulations
Method: Monte Carlo simulations and empirical backtesting comparing Kelly (Full, Half, Triple) vs Markowitz (Tangent, Min Var) vs Equal Weight with daily, weekly, and monthly rebalancing
Findings:
  * Full Kelly maximizes expected growth rate and median terminal wealth in simulations
  * Triple Kelly leads to ruin (losing wealth almost 80% of times in 10,000 trades simulation)
  * Rolling Kelly (2-year window, monthly rebalancing) CAGR 15.01% vs Tangent 10.55% (EuroStoxx50 2007-2018)
  * Kelly portfolio is less diversified (3 assets vs 8 in Tangent) and has higher volatility
  * Short window (2 years) for Kelly optimization outperforms longer windows
Strength: moderate (Uses real market data and Monte Carlo, but relies on estimated returns which are prone to error)
Limits: Transaction costs ignored; assumes normal distribution of returns; estimation risk can lead to ruin; not tested on news signals
For traders: Kelly sizing can boost returns but requires accurate return estimates and high risk tolerance; Half Kelly is safer
For the app: Feature to calculate position sizing based on estimated edge, but warn about estimation risk and recommend Half Kelly

[P4544] How Does the Fortune’s Formula Kelly CapitalGrowth Model Perform? (Leonard C. MacLean, Edward O. Thorp, Yonggan Zhao et al., 2011, The Journal of Portfolio Management, cited by 27, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2011.37.4.096
Question: How do full, fractional, and close to full Kelly capital growth strategies perform in terms of long term gains versus short term risk and the probability of ruin over medium term horizons?
Data: Simulated data based on three simple investment situations; specific markets, years, and sample sizes are not reported in the provided text (only abstract and citing papers available).
Method: The authors simulate the behavior of full Kelly, fractional Kelly, and close to full Kelly strategies over medium term horizons using a large number of scenarios to analyze the trade off between growth and security.
Findings:
  * Full Kelly and close to full Kelly strategies show great superiority over longer horizons, earning very large gains a large fraction of the time.
  * Kelly and high fractional Kelly strategies exhibit very risky short term performance.
  * There is a consistent trade off of growth versus security as a function of the bet size determined by the various strategies.
  * No matter how favorable the opportunities are, a sequence of bad scenarios can lead to very poor final wealth outcomes with a loss of most of the investor's initial capital.
  * In the two asset case (U.S. equity and T bills with annual re balancing), there is a confirmed trade off between terminal wealth and risk: the more aggressive the strategy, the higher the risk.
Strength: moderate (The study uses simulation over many scenarios, but the provided text lacks specific real market data, sample sizes, or actual return figures, relying instead on abstract summaries and second hand citations.)
Limits: The provided text contains only the abstract and citing papers; no specific market data, years, or exact return numbers are available. The results are based on simulations, not historical back testing on specific stock universes. The 'two asset case' mentioned in a citation refers to U.S. equity and T bills, but the main study covers 'three simple investment situations' without further detail in this text.
For traders: While Kelly strategies can maximize long term growth, they carry a high risk of severe short term drawdowns and potential ruin from a string of bad outcomes, suggesting that fractional Kelly (betting less than the full formula suggests) is safer for most investors.
For the app: The app should include a 'risk of ruin' warning when suggesting position sizes based on Kelly criteria, and default to fractional Kelly (e.g., half Kelly) to prevent the 'devastating collapse' described in the findings.

[P4690] Dynamic stop-loss rules as universal performance enhancers (Dimitrios D. Thomakos, Rafael Yahlomi, 2018, Investment Management and Financial Innovations, cited by 1, read from: abstract only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.21511/imfi.15(2).2018.01
Question: Do daily and static stop loss rules improve performance for long and short positions in US equity and bond indices compared to buy and hold and trend following strategies?
Data: US equity and bond indices; sample period not reported in abstract; data source not reported.
Method: The authors test daily and static stop loss rules against buy and hold benchmarks, equally weighted portfolios, and a simple moving average trend following strategy for both long and short positions, checking if stop losses enhance performance while managing risk.
Findings:
  * Daily stop loss rules significantly outperform buy and hold equity and bond benchmarks, equally weighted portfolios, and simple moving average trend following strategies.
  * Longer term stop loss rules help avoid market crashes by exiting the market but cause investors to miss up market days.
  * Shorter term stop loss rules allow investors to stay in the market longer during good days but come at the expense of increased risk and higher drawdowns.
  * Performance enhancements are robust to various variations on the initial theme.
  * Performance improvements can come from sources related to static stop loss rules.
Strength: moderate (The abstract claims robust results across asset classes and strategies, but the lack of specific sample years, return numbers, and cost assumptions limits verification.)
Limits: Only an abstract is available; specific sample years, exact return figures, holding periods, transaction costs, and whether results hold after 2010 are not reported.
For traders: Stop loss rules can improve returns and reduce crash risk, but the optimal duration depends on balancing the need to stay in the market during rallies versus avoiding large drawdowns.
For the app: Implement a configurable stop loss feature that allows users to choose between 'longer term' (crash protection) and 'shorter term' (capture more upside) modes, with a warning about the trade off between missed gains and reduced drawdowns.

[P4691] PERFORMANCE OF STOP-LOSS RULES VS. BUY-AND-HOLD STRATEGY (Garib Yusupov, Bergsveinn Snorrason, 2009, Lund University Publications Student Papers (Lund University), cited by 4, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: http://lup.lub.lu.se/student-papers/record/1474565
Question: Do traditional and trailing stop loss rules outperform a buy and hold strategy for large Swedish stocks over an 11-year period?
Data: Swedish market (OMX Stockholm 30 Index), 54 unique large cap stocks, daily closing prices, January 1998 to April 2009 (approx. 11 years), 45 quarterly holding periods. Data source: Thomson Datastream.
Method: The authors tested two stop loss strategies against a buy and hold (BH) benchmark. They entered the market at an arbitrary start date and held positions for 3-month (quarterly) periods. If a stock's price dropped by a fixed percentage (5% to 55%) from the entry price, the position was sold immediately (Traditional Stop Loss). For the Trailing Stop Loss, the exit price was adjusted upward as the stock price rose but never downward. Proceeds from early exits sat in cash until the next quarter. Returns and variance were compared across equally weighted portfolios.
Findings:
  * Trailing Stop Loss (TSL) at a 15% loss limit achieved the highest cumulative return of 74% over the period, compared to Buy and Hold (BH) which had a cumulative excess return that was substantially negative.
  * Traditional Stop Loss (SL) at a 10% loss limit achieved the highest cumulative return of 57%, with the 15% limit close behind at 53%.
  * The TSL strategy at a 20% loss limit produced the highest average quarterly return of 1.7%, while the SL strategy at 15% produced 1.5%.
  * Stop loss strategies significantly reduced portfolio variance (risk); the 5% TSL limit had a variance of 0.15%, which was ten times lower than the BH strategy's variance of 1.5%.
  * The 5% TSL limit resulted in negative returns (average -0.1%, cumulative -8.1%), indicating that too tight a stop loss can hurt performance in this dataset.
Strength: moderate (The study uses real daily data over a long period (11 years) including a major crash, but the sample is limited to only 30 large Swedish stocks, and the authors admit to potential data mining due to arbitrary start dates and manual Excel calculations.)
Limits: Results are specific to large cap Swedish stocks (OMXS 30) and may not apply to other markets or small caps. The study does not account for transaction costs or slippage (the difference between the stop price and the actual execution price), which would reduce returns. The holding period was fixed at 3 months regardless of when the stop was hit, and cash proceeds were left idle rather than reinvested. The sample size is small (54 stocks total), and the study period ends in 2009, so it does not test performance in the last 15 years.
For traders: Stop loss rules can reduce risk and potentially improve returns for large cap stocks compared to holding through a crash, but setting the limit too tight (e.g., 5%) can cause losses due to normal market noise. A 10-15% limit appears optimal for this specific dataset.
For the app: Implement a 'Risk Adjusted Exit' feature that suggests stop loss levels (e.g., 10-15%) based on the asset's volatility, and warn users that very tight stops (under 10%) may increase the chance of being stopped out by noise rather than a true trend change.

[P4694] On the efficacy of stop-loss rules in the presence of overnight gaps (Argimiro Arratia, Albert Dorador, 2019, Quantitative Finance, cited by 3, read from: full text (CORE))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/14697688.2019.1605188
Question: Do stop loss rules improve risk adjusted returns or absolute returns when accounting for overnight gaps and flash crashes?
Data: 30 highly transacted US stocks (survived 1990-2017), hourly prices, 1990-2017 calibration period, 2017 specific examples
Method: Monte Carlo simulations (5,000 repetitions) using parametric models (Random Walk, ARMA, Regime Switching) and non parametric stationary bootstrap, comparing stop loss vs Buy and Hold
Findings:
  * Fixed percentage rule: Sharpe Ratio multiplied by ~3, Sortino by ~8 in Regime Switching model with gap (Table 3)
  * In rising markets, stop loss improves risk adjusted return but absolute return is slightly lower (usually less than 100 bps drop)
  * In falling markets, stop loss improves absolute expected return (e.g., Ford: 11.3 percentage points higher than Buy and Hold in 2.5 months)
  * Flash crashes trigger Fixed % and ATR rules reducing returns, but RSI and MA crossover rules are robust to flash crashes
  * Overnight gaps make stop loss performance appear better than models without gaps suggest (gaps bypass stops, but modeling them shows the risk)
Strength: moderate (Large sample (30 stocks, 27 years) and multiple models, but relies on simulation and ignores transaction costs)
Limits: Transaction costs and slippage ignored; high frequency data required for accurate gap modeling; US stocks only; no post-2019 evidence
For traders: Stop losses help manage risk and improve risk adjusted returns, but may reduce absolute returns in bull markets and can be bypassed by overnight gaps
For the app: Add a Stop Loss Calculator feature that warns users about overnight gap risk and suggests volatility based (ATR) or trend based (MA) exits over fixed % for robustness

[P4696] Do initial stop-losses stop losses? (Bruce James Vanstone, 2008, Bond University Research Portal (Bond University), cited by 0, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://research.bond.edu.au/files/27693187/2008_Do_initial_stop_losses_stop_losses.pdf
Question: Do initial stop loss rules improve or degrade the long term performance of a trend following trading strategy?
Data: Australian Stock Exchange (ASX200 constituents, including delisted stocks), April 2000 to December 2007, 15,073 trades, transaction costs assumed at $20 each way.
Method: The author tests a simple trend following system (buy when price crosses above the 50-day Exponential Moving Average, sell when it crosses below) on the ASX200. The study compares the portfolio performance of this system with no stops against versions that add initial stop losses set at fixed percentages (1% to 10%) or based on volatility multiples (1x to 5x ATR). Performance is measured by daily mean trade return, average trade duration, and Sharpe ratio.
Findings:
  * The benchmark system (no stops) achieved a Daily Mean Return of $1.76 per trade with an average holding period of 15.85 days.
  * Adding fixed percentage stops (1% to 10%) reduced the Daily Mean Return in every case, with the 1% stop yielding only $0.34 per trade.
  * Adding ATR based stops (1x to 5x ATR) resulted in negative Daily Mean Returns for all tested levels, ranging from -$18.28 (1x ATR) to -$0.54 (5x ATR).
  * The Sharpe ratio for the no stop portfolio was 0.50, while all stop loss variations resulted in lower ratios (e.g., 0.25 for 1% stop, -3.27 for 1x ATR stop).
  * Statistical tests (ANOVA) found no significant difference where stops improved performance; the 1x ATR stop was statistically worse than the no stop strategy.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a large sample of over 15,000 trades and includes delisted stocks to avoid survivorship bias, but it relies on a single, simple strategy and a specific historical period (2000-2007) in one market.)
Limits: The study is limited to the Australian market (ASX200) and the period 2000-2007; it only tests initial stops, not trailing stops; transaction costs are fixed at $20 per trade which may not reflect all retail scenarios; the strategy tested is a simple moving average crossover, not a news based event strategy.
For traders: For a trend following strategy with positive expectation, adding initial stop losses likely degrades returns and increases risk; traders should be cautious about using fixed stops unless they have specific evidence they help their unique system.
For the app: The app should warn users that adding fixed initial stop losses to a positive expectation strategy may reduce overall returns, and suggest that stop loss logic should be validated against the specific strategy's historical data before implementation.

Link: https://doi.org/10.1137/130911706
Question: Does using stop loss and take profit rules improve investment outcomes compared to holding indefinitely, and how should these stops be set?
Data: Theoretical model (arithmetic Brownian motion), parameters: drift mu0=0.15, volatility sigma=0.3, cost c=0.0005.
Method: Mathematical optimization of stopping rules (fixed, trailing, time dependent) under uncertainty about drift.
Findings:
  * Uncertainty about drift justifies using stops (if drift known positive, no lower stop needed).
  * Story (C) (switch funds only on loss) performed best (Objective 20.216 in Table 7).
  * Fixed stops often perform close to optimal stopping rules (e.g., 1.6305 vs 1.6770 in Table 14).
  * Time dependent slopes improve objectives slightly (e.g., Story C improvement 1.7%).
  * Mean trade times vary (e.g., 0.0998 to 0.0125 in Tables 2-7).
Strength: moderate (Rigorous mathematical derivation but lacks empirical validation on real market data.)
Limits: Theoretical model only, no real market data, holding periods in abstract time units.
For traders: Stops protect against bad drift uncertainty; switching funds only after losses yields better results than switching after every stop.
For the app: Feature to calculate optimal stop levels based on news uncertainty; warn against frequent switching.

[P4859] Equity Portfolio Diversification: How Many Stocks are Enough? Evidence from Five Developed Markets (Vitali Alexeev, Francis Tapon, 2012, SSRN Electronic Journal, cited by 27, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2182295
Question: How many stocks are needed in a portfolio to achieve most diversification benefits across five developed markets, and how does this number change during market crises?
Data: Five developed markets (US, UK, Japan, Canada, Australia); 1975 to 2011; daily total return data for common stocks (active and delisted) from Thomson Reuters Datastream; sample filtered for stocks trading at least 75% of days in a year.
Method: The authors simulate random portfolios of increasing size (from 1 stock up to the full market) using daily returns. They calculate risk reduction using three measures: Standard Deviation (SD), Expected Shortfall at 1% (ES1%, an extreme risk measure for black swan events), and Terminal Wealth Standard Deviation (TWSD). They determine the number of stocks required to reduce diversifiable risk by 90% on average, and also calculate the number needed to achieve this reduction 90% of the time (using confidence bands).
Findings:
  * Using Standard Deviation, an average US investor needed 24 stocks (2004-2005) to reduce diversifiable risk by 90%, but needed 56-73 stocks during the 2008-2011 Global Financial Crisis.
  * To achieve a 90% reduction in diversifiable risk 90% of the time in the US using Expected Shortfall (ES1%), a portfolio of 33 to 55 stocks was required for most years, spiking to 63-72 stocks during 2008-2011.
  * Using Terminal Wealth Standard Deviation (TWSD), the US required a relatively constant portfolio of 83-99 stocks to achieve 90% risk reduction.
  * In Japan, the average correlation among stocks was highest (0.16), while in Australia it was lowest (0.07); higher correlations generally meant fewer stocks were needed to diversify.
  * During periods of high market volatility and high correlations (crises), the number of stocks required to assure risk reduction 90% of the time increased significantly compared to calm periods.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a long time series (37 years) across five major markets and includes delisted stocks to avoid survivorship bias, but it relies on simulations rather than a specific trading strategy with transaction costs.)
Limits: The paper provides portfolio construction guidelines (how many stocks to hold) rather than a trading strategy with entry/exit signals; it assumes no transaction costs, taxes, or borrowing; it does not test if these specific portfolio sizes generate excess returns (alpha), only that they reduce risk.
For traders: Individual traders holding fewer than 20 stocks are likely exposed to significant unsystematic risk, especially during crises when correlations rise; holding 30-50 stocks is generally sufficient to capture most diversification benefits for risk reduction.
For the app: Add a 'Diversification Health' metric that compares the user's current portfolio size against the dynamic, crisis adjusted thresholds (e.g., 'You hold 15 stocks; during the 2008 crisis, 63 were needed for 90% risk reduction confidence') to warn users of concentration risk.
Themes: From signal to trade

Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/0015198x.2019.1567190
Question: How do hidden market impact costs from rebalancing affect the expected returns of factor investing strategies, and how can index construction reduce these costs?
Data: Large and long standing factor investing indexes (likely US equities given the journal and authors), period not explicitly stated in abstract, sample size not reported, data source: rebalancing data of factor indexes.
Method: The authors use historical rebalancing data from factor indexes to model implicit market impact costs. They create a framework to attribute these costs to specific strategy characteristics like turnover rate and turnover concentration, then discuss how index construction methods can lower these costs.
Findings:
  * Implicit market impact costs may substantially erode a strategy's expected excess returns (Abstract).
  * Costs are related to liquidity characteristics such as turnover rate and turnover concentration (Citing paper: Is Factor Investing Sustainable after Price Impact Costs? The Capacity of Factor Investing in Korea, 2019).
  * Index construction methods, when thoughtfully designed, can reduce market impact costs (Abstract).
  * Estimates for actual transaction costs vary widely and depend on a variety of factors (Citing paper: Pairs trading in the German stock market: is there still life in the old dog?, 2025).
  * For relatively simple factor strategies, it is difficult to provide accurate estimates of these costs (Citing paper: On the performance of factor investing: an analysis based on constant mix and buy and hold strategies, 2025).
Strength: moderate (The study uses real rebalancing data from established indexes to model costs, but the full text is unavailable to verify specific return figures or cost assumptions.)
Limits: Only the abstract and citing sentences are available; specific numerical results, exact sample years, and the detailed 'framework' for cost attribution are not reported. The findings rely on second hand descriptions from citing papers for some details.
For traders: Retail traders using factor based strategies must account for hidden rebalancing costs, which can significantly eat into profits, especially for strategies with high turnover or concentrated trades.
For the app: The app should include a 'cost estimator' feature that flags news driven storylines involving high turnover stocks or sectors, warning users that frequent rebalancing might erase the expected gains from the event.

[P5034] Chinese securities investment funds: the role of luck in performance (Jun Gao, Niall O’Sullivan, Meadhbh Sherman, 2021, Review of Accounting and Finance, cited by 70, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1108/raf-07-2020-0182
Question: Does the performance of Chinese mutual fund managers come from genuine skill or just luck?
Data: Chinese open end equity funds, May 2003 to September 2020, sample size over 50 risk adjusted models tested, data source not explicitly named in abstract but implies fund performance databases.
Method: Used a non parametric bootstrap method on fund returns to separate skill from luck, accounting for non normal risk and testing over 50 different risk adjusted models to find the best fit.
Findings:
  * The evidence does not support the existence of 'genuine' skilled fund managers.
  * Top ranked funds with positive abnormal performance are attributed to 'good luck' rather than 'good skill'.
  * Poor performance in bottom funds is mainly due to 'bad skill' (bad stock picking).
  * Survivorship bias (dropping failed funds from data) was a concern addressed in the study design.
  * Findings are robust across different sub periods and market conditions.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a robust bootstrap methodology and tests many models over a long period (2003-2020), but the full text is not available to verify specific return numbers or cost assumptions.)
Limits: Only the abstract and citing sentences are available; specific return percentages, exact sample counts of funds, and detailed cost assumptions are not reported. The findings are specific to the Chinese fund market and may not apply to other countries. The citing papers mostly discuss green finance or macroeconomics and do not add specific data about the fund performance results.
For traders: Individual investors should not try to pick 'winning' funds based on past performance as top results are likely luck, but they should avoid 'losing' funds as poor results often reflect bad skill.
For the app: Add a warning feature that flags 'hot' funds (top performers) as likely luck driven and suggests avoiding them, while highlighting 'cold' funds (bottom performers) as likely skill driven and recommending avoidance.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5041] Mutual Fund Performance: Skill Or Luck? (Dirk Nitzsche, Keith Cuthbertson, Niall O’Sullivan, 2005, RePEc: Research Papers in Economics, cited by 4, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: http://repec.org/mmfc05/paper4.pdf
Question: Can a trader distinguish whether a mutual fund's past success is due to genuine stock picking skill or simply good luck, and does this ability persist?
Data: UK equity mutual funds (surviving and non surviving), April 1975 to December 2002, sample of over 1,500 funds (724 with at least 60 months of data), data from Fenchurch Corporate Services using Standard & Poor's Analytical Software.
Method: The authors use a cross sectional bootstrap methodology to simulate a 'luck distribution' for fund performance (specifically the t statistic of alpha) under the null hypothesis that no fund has skill. They compare actual fund performance against this simulated distribution to determine if top or bottom performers are statistically significant outliers that cannot be explained by chance alone, while controlling for non normal risks and using the Fama French 3-factor model.
Findings:
  * The best performing fund achieved an abnormal return of 0.745% per month (8.94% per year) with a t statistic of 4.023, but the bootstrap p value was 0.056, meaning it marginally fails to reject the hypothesis that this result was due to luck alone.
  * At the negative end of the performance scale, the analysis strongly rejects the hypothesis that poor funds are merely unlucky; these funds demonstrate 'bad skill'.
  * Genuine stock picking ability was found in a small number of top performing 'equity income' and 'equity growth' funds, but not in 'small stock' or 'general equity' funds.
  * Positive performance in 'onshore' funds was attributed to genuine skill, whereas positive performance in 'offshore' funds was attributed to luck.
  * The average risk adjusted abnormal performance across the entire industry was negative or zero, consistent with the view that most active managers underperform after costs.
Strength: strong (The study uses a comprehensive dataset including non surviving funds (avoiding survivorship bias) and a robust non parametric bootstrap method to handle non normal return distributions, covering a long 27-year period.)
Limits: The study focuses exclusively on UK mutual funds from 1975 to 2002; results may not apply to other markets, time periods, or individual stock trading. The 'best' fund result was only marginally significant (p=0.056), and the paper does not provide specific entry/exit rules for individual stocks.
For traders: Individual investors should be skeptical of past winners as they are often just lucky, but should be wary of consistent losers as they likely possess 'bad skill' and will continue to underperform.
For the app: The app should implement a 'skill vs. luck' filter that uses bootstrapping or similar statistical tests on a fund's or stock's track record to warn users when a recent winning streak is statistically indistinguishable from random noise.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5044] An Empirical Investigation of the Performance of Japanese Mutual Funds: Skill or Luck? (Keith Pılbeam, Hamish Preston, 2019, International Journal of Financial Studies, cited by 20, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijfs7010006
Question: Do Japanese mutual fund managers possess genuine skill in selecting stocks or timing the market, or are their results simply due to luck?
Data: 355 actively managed Japanese Equity Mutual Funds, Japan, April 2011 to April 2016
Method: The authors compared fund performance against a four factor capital asset pricing model benchmark using equal weighted portfolios and Jensen's alpha. They tested market timing ability using the Treynor and Mazuy measure and applied a cross sectional bootstrap to handle non normal data distribution.
Findings:
  * Japanese Mutual Funds fail to outperform the benchmark four factor capital asset pricing model based on equal weight portfolio and Jensen's alpha measures.
  * 33 funds showed significant positive market timing ability, while 31 funds showed significant negative timing ability, largely offsetting each other.
  * A large proportion of funds fail to outperform a hypothetical world with no skill, even after correcting for non normality using Fama and French's cross sectional bootstrap.
  * There is stronger persistence for poor performing funds than for strong performing funds.
  * About 9.30% of the funds were identified as having market timing ability (as noted in citing papers summarizing the T M model results).
Strength: moderate (The study uses a robust statistical method (bootstrap) to address data non normality, but the sample is limited to one country (Japan) and a specific 5-year period.)
Limits: Data is limited to the abstract and second hand citations; full text details on specific return percentages, transaction costs, or exact sample size breakdowns are not available. The study focuses on mutual funds, not individual stock trading or news based strategies.
For traders: Individual investors should be skeptical that active fund managers can consistently beat the market through skill, as poor performance tends to persist while good performance does not.
For the app: nothing
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5045] U.S. Mutual Fund Performance: Skill or Luck? (Kenneth Nordlund Hoem, Erik Rosmer Aasland, 2018, NORA - Norwegian Open Research Archives, cited by 0, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: http://hdl.handle.net/11250/2579105
Question: How can a trader distinguish whether mutual fund performance comes from genuine skill or random luck, and what does the data say about the existence of skilled managers after costs?
Data: 1,704 actively managed U.S. open end domestic equity mutual funds; January 1995 to December 2017; data source not explicitly named in abstract but implies standard fund return databases (e.g., CRSP/Center for Research in Security Prices).
Method: The authors use regression analysis to test if fund managers, on average, beat the market after costs. They then use a 'bootstrap' procedure (a computer simulation that reshuffles data to create a 'luck' baseline) to see how many funds performed better than pure chance would allow. They test this using both net returns (after fees) and gross returns (before fees).
Findings:
  * Regression results for an equal weighted portfolio suggest that fund managers in aggregate do not possess sufficient skill to cover their costs.
  * Bootstrap results show that a sizeable minority of fund managers do have sufficient skill to cover their costs.
  * The evidence of skill is stronger when examining performance gross of management fees.
  * Under the assumption that true alpha follows a normal distribution, the standard deviation (sigma) for the left tail (unskilled) is about 0.75% a year.
  * Under the same assumption, the standard deviation (sigma) for the right tail (skilled) is about 1.25% a year.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a large sample size (1,704 funds) and a robust statistical method (bootstrap) to separate luck from skill, though it relies on the assumption of a normal distribution for true alpha which may not perfectly reflect reality.)
Limits: The provided text is only an abstract and second hand citations; specific details on the exact regression models, cost assumptions, or the definition of 'sizeable minority' are not fully detailed. The citing papers frequently confuse this 2018 paper with a 2008 paper by Cuthbertson et al. regarding UK funds, so care must be taken to distinguish the findings. The results are specific to U.S. mutual funds and may not apply to individual stock picking.
For traders: Individual investors should be skeptical that most active managers can beat the market after fees, but a small group of skilled managers does exist; however, identifying them in advance is difficult as past performance often includes a luck component.
For the app: nothing
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5046] Reassessing False Discoveries in Mutual Fund Performance: Skill, Luck, or Lack of Power? (Angie Andrikogiannopoulou, Filippos Papakonstantinou, 2019, The Journal of Finance, cited by 56, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12784
Question: Does the False Discovery Rate (FDR) methodology accurately distinguish between skilled mutual fund managers and those who got lucky, or does it fail due to low statistical power in noisy data?
Data: U.S. equity mutual funds, CRSP Survivorship Bias Free database, 1975 to 2006 (extended to 2011 in robustness checks), sample size of 1,400 funds in balanced panels and 2,076 in unbalanced panels, monthly return data.
Method: The authors run simulations using real world mutual fund data parameters (returns, factor loadings, errors) to generate synthetic fund performance. They then apply the False Discovery Rate (FDR) statistical test to these synthetic datasets to see if it correctly identifies the known proportions of skilled (positive alpha), unskilled (negative alpha), and zero skill funds. They vary the 'signal to noise' ratio by changing the size of the true alpha and the number of years of data per fund.
Findings:
  * The FDR method misclassifies 65% of funds with economically large alphas of ±2% per year as having zero alpha (no skill).
  * In simulations where the true proportion of zero alpha funds was 1%, the FDR method estimated it to be 70%.
  * The accuracy of the FDR method does not improve by adding more funds to the sample (large N); it only improves by adding more years of data per fund (large T), and even then, convergence is very slow.
  * The method assumes that p values above a certain threshold come only from zero skill funds, but in reality, low skill funds also produce p values in this range, causing the method to overestimate the number of zero skill funds.
  * Realistic levels of correlation between funds increase the variability of the FDR estimates by 2.5 to 2.8 times compared to assuming funds are independent.
Strength: strong (The study uses extensive simulations calibrated with real market data (CRSP) and tests a wide range of realistic scenarios, directly challenging a widely used statistical method in finance.)
Limits: The paper focuses entirely on the statistical validity of a performance evaluation method (FDR) for mutual funds; it does not propose a specific trading strategy, nor does it test individual stock trading or news based events.
For traders: Individual traders should be skeptical of studies claiming 'most funds have zero skill' based on FDR tests, as these tests likely miss many skilled managers due to data noise; however, this paper does not provide a new way to pick stocks.
For the app: nothing

Question: How can a trader distinguish whether the returns of active fund managers are due to genuine skill or just random luck?

The analysis is on net returns (after fees), so it cannot separate gross skill from fee structures.
For traders: Individual investors should be skeptical of short track records, as luck can easily mimic skill in small samples; however, the worst performers are likely genuinely bad, so avoiding the bottom tier is a valid strategy.

Method: The authors calculate a 'Fund Herding' score for each fund by regressing the fund's trades against past aggregate institutional trades, controlling for stock characteristics. Findings:

  * Funds with a herding tendency 1.65 standard deviations above average underperform those 1.65 standard deviations below average by 11 basis points per month (1.32% per year).

Limits: The study focuses exclusively on US mutual funds; it does not test if individual retail investors can replicate this by picking stocks directly, nor does it provide data on transaction costs for implementing a strategy based on fund holdings (which are reported quarterly).

For the app: Add a 'Herding Score' metric to fund profiles; flag funds with high positive scores as 'Low Skill/High Imitation' and suggest avoiding them or shorting them if possible.

Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-036x.2009.00536.x
Question: How can an investor distinguish between genuine skill and luck when evaluating the performance of many mutual funds, and what is the true proportion of winners and losers after correcting for multiple hypothesis testing?
Data: UK equity mutual funds (Unit Trusts and OEICs), April 1975 to December 2002, sample of 675 funds with at least 36 months of data, data source: Fenchurch Corporate Services (S&P Analytical Software).
Method: The authors use a False Discovery Rate (FDR) framework to test the alphas of 675 funds simultaneously. Instead of treating each fund's performance test in isolation (which leads to many false positives), they estimate the proportion of funds that are truly null (no skill) and calculate the expected percentage of 'significant' funds that are actually lucky. They form portfolios of 'best' and 'worst' funds based on a controlled FDR threshold (e.g., 10%) to see if these groups generate genuine abnormal returns.
Findings:
  * At a 10% significance level, the False Discovery Rate (FDR) for the best performing funds is 67%, meaning only about 2% of all funds truly outperform their benchmarks.
  * For the worst performing funds, the FDR is relatively low at 15.9%, resulting in 20% of all funds truly underperforming their benchmarks.
  * When controlling the overall FDR at a 10% threshold, a portfolio of the 'best' funds (approx. 10-20 funds) generates an expected alpha between 4.57% and 10.1% per annum.
  * A portfolio of the 'worst' funds (approx. 40-85 funds) selected under the same 10% FDR threshold generates an expected alpha of approximately -3.6% per annum.
  * The pattern of very few genuine winners and a larger number of genuine losers holds across different investment styles (all companies, small companies, and equity income), though equity income funds show fewer genuine losers.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large, comprehensive sample of the entire UK mutual fund universe over a long period (27 years) and applies a rigorous statistical framework (FDR) that corrects for the high probability of false positives inherent in testing hundreds of funds simultaneously.)
Limits: The data ends in 2002, so it does not show if these patterns hold in the post-2002 era; the results are specific to the UK market and mutual fund structure; the study focuses on identifying skill in funds rather than trading individual stocks based on news events.
For traders: Individual traders should be extremely skeptical of short term 'winning' stocks or funds, as most apparent outperformance is likely luck; however, identifying consistent underperformers is more reliable, and avoiding them can generate value.
For the app: The app should implement a 'False Discovery' filter: when the app identifies a potential 'winner' story, it should flag that the probability of this being a false positive is high (e.g., >60%) unless the signal is extremely strong, and prioritize 'loser' stories as they are more likely to be genuine.

[P5200] Split-Sample Strategies for Avoiding False Discoveries (Michael Anderson, Jeremy Magruder, 2017, National Bureau of Economic Research, cited by 62, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3386/w23544
Question: How can researchers avoid false discoveries when testing many hypotheses by splitting data into exploratory and confirmation samples, and how does this compare to pre registration?
Data: Re analysis of the GoBiFo community driven development field experiment (Casey et al., 2012); sample includes 334 candidate dependent variables and 183 core variables from village level data; no stock market data, returns, or trading periods involved.
Method: The authors simulate splitting a dataset into an exploratory sample (to generate hypotheses) and a confirmation sample (to test them). They compare this 'split sample' approach against 'Preanalysis Plans' (PAPs, where hypotheses are fixed before seeing data) and a 'hybrid' approach (fixing high priority hypotheses while using split sampling for others). They calculate the probability of finding true effects (power) and controlling false positives under different split ratios and significance thresholds.
Findings:
  * An optimized split sample approach achieves 90% of the statistical power of an optimal Preanalysis Plan (PAP) without requiring preregistration.
  * In a specific simulation with one true effect and 19 null hypotheses, setting a low pass threshold (t statistic of 1) and using a small exploratory sample (26% of data) increased power by 39% compared to a standard 50/50 split with a higher threshold.
  * Re analyzing the GoBiFo data with a hybrid approach would have identified that the program increased local governance participation (a 'software' outcome) with a full sample t statistic of 4.4, which was missed by the original PAP.
  * The hybrid approach revealed meaningful heterogeneity: the program was more effective in smaller villages and in villages with an 'extractive chief,' findings that were not robust under the original PAP.
  * Under a hybrid approach with False Discovery Rate (FDR) control, there was a 51-58% chance of identifying that larger villages were less effective at improving infrastructure, a finding missed by pure PAPs.
Strength: moderate (The paper uses rigorous simulations and a real world field experiment re analysis, but the results are specific to social science field experiments, not financial markets.)
Limits: The paper focuses entirely on field experiments in development economics (village level data); it contains no data on stock prices, trading costs, holding periods, or financial returns. The 'methods' section explicitly lists 'none' for trading strategies.
For traders: This paper offers no direct trading strategy; it teaches that if you test many ideas on historical data, you will find false patterns by luck unless you reserve a portion of your data to confirm your best ideas.
For the app: Implement a 'Holdout Validator' feature: when the app identifies a potential storyline, it must withhold the most recent data (e.g., the last 20% of the timeline) to confirm the pattern holds before recommending a trade, preventing the app from overfitting to noise.

[P5341] The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality (David H. Bailey, Marcos López de Prado, 2014, The Journal of Portfolio Management, cited by 119, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2014.40.5.094
Question: How can a trader determine if a strategy's good backtest results are due to skill or luck, and how to correct for testing many ideas?
Data: Theoretical and simulation based study; no specific market, country, or historical sample of real trades is used. The authors use numerical experiments and mathematical derivations to model the effects of multiple testing and non normal returns.
Method: The paper proposes the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR), a statistical formula that adjusts a strategy's reported Sharpe ratio downward based on the number of independent trials (backtests) run, the variance of those trials, and the skewness/kurtosis of the returns. It also suggests a 'secretary problem' rule to limit the number of trials to avoid overfitting.
Findings:
  * As the number of independent trials (N) increases, the expected maximum Sharpe ratio of the 'best' strategy increases purely by chance, even if the true skill is zero.
  * In a numerical example, a strategy with an annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.5 over 5 years (1,250 days) was deemed statistically insignificant (only 90% confidence) because it resulted from 88 independent trials.
  * If the same strategy had been the result of only 46 independent trials, it would have been considered significant (above 95% confidence).
  * Non normal returns (skewness and kurtosis) further inflate performance estimates, making it harder to distinguish skill from luck.
  * The optimal number of trials to test before selecting a strategy is approximately 37% (1/e) of the total set of theoretically justifiable configurations, following the 'secretary problem' logic.
Strength: strong (The paper provides rigorous mathematical proofs and numerical simulations to quantify the impact of selection bias and non normality on performance metrics.)
Limits: The paper is purely methodological and theoretical; it does not test a specific trading strategy on real market data, nor does it report actual returns, holding periods, or trading costs for any asset class.
For traders: Individual traders must track how many variations of an idea they test; a high Sharpe ratio is likely luck if it comes from testing hundreds of variations, and they should stop testing after finding a strategy that beats the best of a random 37% sample.
For the app: The app should include a 'Backtest Overfitting Risk' metric that calculates the Deflated Sharpe Ratio for any storyline it generates, requiring the user to input or estimate the number of alternative storylines considered to adjust the confidence level.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5342] The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: A Unified Framework for Search-Adjusted Performance Inference (Marcos López de Prado, Emilio Porcu, 2026, The Journal of Portfolio Management, cited by 0, read from: abstract only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2026.070
Question: How can a trader distinguish between genuine skill and luck when a strategy is the result of searching through many possible models or parameters?

Method: The paper proposes a statistical framework called the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) to adjust performance metrics based on the number of trials (search) conducted. It offers three versions: DSR L for a basic benchmark, DSR LS for a more detailed analysis including dispersion, and DSR EO for exact tail inference, all designed to calculate the probability that a 'winning' strategy is actually just a statistical fluke.
Findings:
  * The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) addresses the problem that a strategy selected after searching many options cannot be evaluated as if it were pre specified.
  * DSR L provides a parsimonious location benchmark for determining if a result is significant after accounting for the search process.
  * DSR LS adds the dispersion of the selected maximum to support power analysis and minimum track record calculations.
  * DSR EO uses the complete search distribution when exact tail inference is available.
  * The shape of the return distribution (Gaussian vs. Student t) can alter both the magnitude and direction of approximation errors in performance evaluation.
Strength: moderate (The paper unifies existing implementations and derives general calibration results, but the abstract only describes the framework without reporting empirical test results or specific return numbers.)
Limits: Only the abstract is available; no specific market data, sample sizes, holding periods, or backtest results are provided. The findings are theoretical and methodological rather than empirical.
For traders: Before trusting a strategy that performed well, you must adjust your confidence based on how many other strategies you tested to find it; the more you searched, the less likely the result is due to skill.
For the app: Implement a 'Search Penalty' metric that reduces the reported confidence score of any strategy based on the number of variations (parameters, news triggers, or holding periods) the user or the system tested to find it.

[P5343] Practical Applications of The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality (David H. Bailey, Marcos López de Prado, 2015, Practical Applications, cited by 0, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/pa.2015.2.3.089
Question: How can a trader distinguish between genuine skill and luck caused by testing too many ideas, and what statistical tools correct for this bias?
Data: No specific market, country, or sample size data is provided in the text; the paper is a theoretical and methodological report on the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) derived from general financial principles.
Method: The paper proposes a statistical tool called the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) to adjust performance metrics. It accounts for three main causes of 'performance inflation': selection bias (testing many strategies and only reporting the best), non normality of returns (skewed or fat tailed distributions), and short sample lengths. It suggests that the required length of a backtest increases with the number of trials performed.
Findings:
  * The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) adjusts the observed Sharpe ratio based on the number of trials (N), the variance of the trials' Sharpe ratios, and the non normality (skewness and kurtosis) of the return series.
  * A strategy selected as the best among many specifications has an upward biased performance estimate, where the bias grows with the number of specifications tried and shrinks with the length of the evaluation window.
  * High simulated performance is easily achievable after backtesting relatively few strategy configurations due to memory effects in financial series, leading to systematic under performance in live trading.
  * The paper introduces the concept of 'Minimum Backtest Length' (MinBTL) to determine the sample size required to avoid selecting a strategy that looks good in sample but fails out of sample.
  * Citing papers note that without DSR adjustment, a Sharpe ratio computed on a sample without accounting for the number of trials that produced the winning trades will overstate the strategy's true skill.
Strength: moderate (The paper provides a rigorous mathematical framework for correcting selection bias, but the provided text is limited to an abstract and second hand citations, lacking the original empirical data or specific backtest results from the paper itself.)
Limits: The provided text consists only of an abstract and sentences from other papers citing this work; no original data, specific market samples, or detailed results from the 2015 paper are included in the input.
For traders: Individual traders must assume that any strategy found after testing many variations is likely a statistical fluke unless the backtest is extremely long or the strategy is adjusted for the number of trials performed.
For the app: The app should include a 'search pressure' metric that counts how many news event combinations or storylines were tested before selecting the final signal, and automatically adjust the confidence score of the recommendation downward if the search space was large.

[P5351] In-Sample and Out-of-Sample Sharpe Ratios for Linear Predictive Models (Antoine Jacquier, Johannes Muhle‐Karbe, Mulligan, Joseph, 2025, RePEc: Research Papers in Economics, cited by 1, read from: full text (arXiv))
Link: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2501.03938
Question: How much does in sample performance overestimate out of sample performance due to overfitting in linear predictive models?
Data: Commodity futures (12 assets), US Equity Index (CRSP), 1926 to 2024, 5,000,000 resamples, simulation of 13 years (10 in sample, 3 out of sample)
Method: Fit linear models (OLS or ridge) on in sample data to predict returns, then test on out of sample data to compare Sharpe ratios (risk adjusted return measure) and calculate the replication ratio (out of sample Sharpe divided by in sample Sharpe).
Findings:
  * Replication ratio diminishes for complex strategies with many assets and many weak signals.
  * Replication ratio increases when more training data is used.
  * Panel regression (simpler model) had 68% replication ratio vs 9% for full model on real data.
  * Panel out of sample Sharpe ratio was 0.5 vs 0.3 for full model (full model in sample was 3.6).
  * Low true Sharpe ratio signals are particularly vulnerable to overfitting.
Strength: strong (Combines analytical formulas with large scale simulation (5 million resamples) and empirical data up to 2024.)
Limits: Transaction costs not reported; commodity futures not stocks; holding periods vary (daily/monthly); paper is 2025 so no post publication evidence.
For traders: Simple models with long data histories are less likely to be luck; complex models with many signals often fail out of sample.
For the app: Add a 'replication ratio' warning metric to alert users when a storyline relies on too many weak signals or short data history.
