[P5887] On Market Timing and Investment Performance. II. Statistical Procedures for Evaluating Forecasting Skills (Roy D. Henriksson, Robert C. Merton, 1981, The Journal of Business, cited by 1,321, read from: citing papers only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1086/296144
Question: How can a statistical test distinguish between a fund manager's genuine skill in predicting market direction and results caused by random luck?
Data: The provided text consists only of 70 sentences from citing papers (2018–2023) referencing the 1981 study; the original paper's specific market, sample size, and years are not reported in the text.
Method: The paper proposes a statistical procedure (regression based and nonparametric) to evaluate if a manager can predict whether market returns will be above or below the risk free rate, using a dummy variable that equals 1 when the market return is positive and 0 otherwise to test for timing ability.
Findings:
  * According to a 2019 study citing this paper, the ability to time the market was found in roughly 2.5% of mutual funds.
  * A 2022 study citing this paper notes that Henriksson (1984) later validated the model and discovered that only 3 out of 116 funds had significant market timing ability.
  * The model assumes managers use qualitative approaches to predict if market returns will be greater or less than the risk free rate.
  * The test distinguishes between 'macroforecasting skills' (market timing) and 'microforecasting skills' (security selection).
  * Later research cited in the text indicates that the model's error terms are often serially correlated and heteroscedastic, which can affect the accuracy of the skill assessment if not corrected.
Strength: moderate (The method is widely cited and applied across decades and markets, but the specific data and results of the original 1981 paper are not present in the provided text, relying instead on second hand descriptions.)
Limits: The provided text contains no original data, sample sizes, or specific return figures from the 1981 paper; all findings are summaries from later studies, and the original paper's specific market conditions and time periods are not reported.
For traders: Individual traders should be skeptical of short track records showing market timing success, as statistical tests suggest such skills are extremely rare (found in only ~2.5% of funds) and often indistinguishable from luck.
For the app: The app should include a 'luck vs. skill' calculator that uses the Henriksson Merton logic (or similar nonparametric tests) to evaluate a trader's own directional calls over time, warning them if their success rate is statistically indistinguishable from random guessing.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5945] Anomalous Price Behavior Around Repurchase Tender Offers (Josef Lakonishok, Theo Vermaelen, 1990, The Journal of Finance, cited by 400, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1990.tb03698.x
Question: Do stock prices drift upward following repurchase tender offers, and what are the returns for strategies buying before expiration or holding long term?
Data: US markets (NYSE, AMEX, OTC), 1962-1986, 258 repurchase tender offers (221 with full data), data from CRSP, CUPV, S&P Daily Stock Price Record, and SEC filings.
Method: The authors test two approaches: 1) A short term strategy buying shares before the tender offer expires when the market price is at least 3% (or 5%) below the tender offer price, then selling non repurchased shares shortly after expiration. 2) A long term strategy holding the stock of companies that announced a repurchase for up to 24 months after the announcement, comparing returns against various benchmarks (value weighted, equally weighted, size matched, and size/beta matched).
Findings:
  * Buying shares before expiration when the price is at least 3% below the tender offer price generated an average abnormal return of 9.61% over a period of less than one week (1962-1986).
  * The degree of underpricing explains more than 75% of the return variability; a 1% discount relative to the tender price results in approximately 0.85% abnormal return.
  * Repurchasing firms outperformed the value weighted index by 23.11% (cumulative) from month 3 to month 24 after the announcement (1962-1986).
  * Small firms (size quintile 1) generated cumulative abnormal returns of 47.02% from one month prior to 24 months after the repurchase, while large firms (quintile 5) generated 15.18%.
  * In the second subperiod (1980-1986), the short term strategy still yielded high returns (e.g., 11.26% average abnormal return), but the long term post expiration drift for large firms dropped to near zero (0.34% cumulative for quintile 5).
Strength: strong (The study uses a comprehensive dataset of 258 events over 24 years with rigorous statistical testing, though the sample is limited to a specific historical period.)
Limits: Data is from 1962-1986; the paper does not report trading costs explicitly (though notes cash settlement is expensive for small trades); long term results are highly sensitive to the benchmark used (value weighted vs. equally weighted); the strategy requires access to tender offer terms and expiration dates which may be harder to track now.
For traders: A retail trader could profit by buying shares of companies with active tender offers when the market price is significantly below the offer price, but holding the stock long term is only profitable for small cap firms, not large ones.
For the app: The app should flag repurchase tender offers and calculate the discount between the current market price and the tender price; if the discount is >3%, it should trigger a 'buy' signal with a short holding period, and separately flag small cap repurchasers for a potential long term hold.

Link: https://doi.org/10.1086/209724
Question: What are the long term abnormal returns for stocks following forward and reverse split announcements, and how do these returns relate to dividend changes?
Data: US stock market, 1976 to 1991, sample of 5,596 stock splits and 76 reverse splits, data source not explicitly named in abstract but implied to be CRSP/Compustat standard for the era.
Method: The authors calculate buy and hold abnormal returns (BHAR) for individual stocks over one and three years following the announcement month, comparing them to a benchmark to measure underreaction.
Findings:
  * For stock splits, the average one year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is 7.05%.
  * For stock splits, the average three year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is 11.87%.
  * For reverse splits, the average one year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is -10.76%.
  * For reverse splits, the average three year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is -33.90%.
  * The positive returns for splits are positively associated with an increase in dividends announced at the same time.
Strength: moderate (Large sample size (5,596 splits) and clear methodology, but the data period ends in 1991, which is over 30 years ago.)
Limits: The study only covers data up to 1991; no evidence is provided on whether these returns persist after 1991 or in recent decades. The text does not specify transaction costs or exact entry timing relative to the announcement (e.g., day of vs. day after).
For traders: A retail trader could potentially profit by buying stocks that announce a split and holding for 1-3 years, or shorting reverse splits, but must be aware that these results are from a pre-2000 market and costs may eat into the 7-11% annual gains.
For the app: The app should flag 'Stock Split' and 'Reverse Split' as high confidence storylines; for splits, link the event to a 'dividend increase' check to strengthen the signal, and for reverse splits, treat it as a strong negative signal.

[P5951] The Information in Management’s Expected Earnings Report Date: A Day Late, a Penny Short (Mark E. Bagnoli, William J. Kross, Susan G. Watts, 2002, Journal of Accounting Research, cited by 180, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679x.t01-1-00054
Question: How much of the negative news associated with delayed earnings reports is priced in on the day the expected date passes versus over the following days and weeks?
Data: US stocks, 1995 to July 1998, sample of 25,934 quarterly earnings announcements from 4,434 firms, data from First Call (Thomson Financial), Compustat, and CRSP.
Method: The authors compare actual earnings report dates to management's voluntarily disclosed expected dates. They calculate market adjusted returns (stock return minus S&P 500 return) starting one day before the expected date and continuing through the actual announcement. They also analyze the relationship between the number of days late and the size of the earnings surprise (actual earnings minus analyst consensus forecast).
Findings:
  * Management's expected dates are 73.8% accurate on average, rising to 80.6% by 1998, compared to less than 33% accuracy for statistical models.
  * For every day an announcement is delayed, the average earnings surprise becomes more negative by approximately one penny per share (e.g., -0.011 for 1-3 days late vs -0.049 for 4+ days late).
  * Average cumulative market adjusted returns for stocks missing their expected date are negative and significant: -0.3% by the second day late, -0.7% by the third day, and -1.0% by the fourth day.
  * Analysts rarely revise their earnings forecasts (91% of the time) immediately after a missed expected date, even though investors react by selling.
  * The market continues to adjust prices downward as the delay lengthens, indicating that the full impact of the bad news is not priced in on the day the expected date passes.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (25,934 observations) over a multi year period with clear statistical significance in both earnings surprises and market returns.)
Limits: Data is limited to 1995-1998; the study does not report trading costs or net returns after fees; the sample is restricted to firms covered by First Call (typically larger, analyst covered firms).
For traders: A missed expected earnings date is a reliable early warning signal of bad news, but the full price drop happens gradually over several days, not all at once.
For the app: Add a feature that tracks 'Expected Report Date' vs 'Actual Date' and alerts users when a date is missed, predicting a continued downward trend in price and earnings estimates over the next 3-5 days.

[P5969] Improved Methods for Tests of Long‐Run Abnormal Stock Returns (John D. Lyon, Brad M. Barber, Chih‐Ling Tsai, 1999, The Journal of Finance, cited by 1,826, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00101
Question: How can researchers correctly test for long run abnormal stock returns without statistical errors caused by data biases?
Data: US stock market (CRSP data), 1973 to 1993, sample includes 14 size portfolios and 10 book to market portfolios; data source is CRSP.
Method: The paper compares two main approaches to test if stocks earn abnormal returns over long periods (1, 3, or 5 years). First, it uses an event study framework with buy and hold returns, correcting for biases by matching firms to reference portfolios based on size and book to market, and using special statistics (bootstrapped skewness adjusted t statistic or empirical p values) to handle skewed data. Second, it uses calendar time portfolios where a portfolio is formed every month and tracked over time, using a standard time series t statistic. The paper simulates these methods on random and non random samples to see which ones give accurate results.
Findings:
  * Rebalancing bias causes returns on small firm portfolios to be overstated by more than 10 percent per year when calculated with monthly rebalancing compared to buy and hold.
  * Rebalancing bias causes returns on high book to market portfolios to be overstated by 3 to 4 percent per year.
  * Using buy and hold reference portfolios eliminates the new listing and rebalancing biases, ensuring the population mean abnormal return is zero by construction.
  * In random samples, the bootstrapped skewness adjusted t statistic and empirical p value methods yield well specified test statistics (correct rejection rates near 5%).
  * In non random samples with industry clustering or overlapping returns, even improved methods may fail to fully correct for cross sectional dependence, making calendar time portfolio methods a preferred alternative in those specific cases.
Strength: strong (The paper uses extensive simulations on 20 years of real market data to prove that common methods are statistically flawed and provides specific, tested corrections.)
Limits: The study focuses on statistical correctness of tests rather than providing a specific trading strategy with profit numbers; it does not test performance after 1993; it notes that cross sectional dependence (e.g., many firms in the same industry) can still cause errors even with the improved methods.
For traders: Individual traders should not trust simple backtests of long term news strategies that use monthly rebalanced benchmarks, as they likely overstate returns by 3-10% annually; they must use buy and hold benchmarks and account for the fact that long term returns are skewed.
For the app: The app must calculate returns using a 'buy and hold' logic for both the stock and the benchmark (no monthly rebalancing of the benchmark) and use empirical p values or skewness adjusted statistics to determine if a news driven strategy is truly skillful or just lucky.
Themes: Skill or luck

[P5972] Individual Investor Trading and Stock Returns (Ron Kaniel, Gideon Saar, Sheridan D. Titman, 2008, The Journal of Finance, cited by 1,013, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01316.x
Question: Do short term return reversals following intense net individual trading generate excess returns after accounting for past returns and volume?
Data: NYSE stocks, 2,034 stocks, 1,004 trading days (sample period not explicitly stated in text but data source is NYSE CAUD files, likely late 1990s to early 2000s based on context of other cited works like 1991-1996), data source: NYSE Consolidated Equity Audit Trail Data (CAUD).
Method: The authors calculate a Net Individual Trading (NIT) measure for each stock weekly. They sort stocks into deciles based on NIT intensity. They then measure the market adjusted returns over the 20 days following weeks of intense buying (top decile) and intense selling (bottom decile), controlling for past returns and turnover.
Findings:
  * Stocks experience statistically significant excess returns of 0.80% in the 20 days following a week of intense buying by individuals.
  * Stocks experience statistically significant excess returns of -0.33% in the 20 days following a week of intense individual selling.
  * The mean market adjusted return in the 20 days prior to a week of intense individual selling is 3.15%, while prior to intense buying it is -2.47%.
  * Excess returns are larger in less liquid stocks: the 20-day excess return on the intense buying portfolio is 1.40% for stocks with large effective spreads (least liquid) versus 0.42% for stocks with small effective spreads (most liquid).
  * The return patterns are distinct from and not subsumed by past return or volume effects, as NIT remains a significant predictor in regressions controlling for these factors.
Strength: moderate (The study uses high quality proprietary NYSE order level data to precisely identify individual trades, but the sample period is not explicitly defined in the provided text, and the strategy relies on a specific market microstructure mechanism (liquidity provision) that may be hard for retail to repl)
Limits: The specific start and end years of the 1,004 trading day sample are not reported in the text; the strategy relies on identifying 'intense' trading which requires granular order flow data not typically available to retail investors; returns are reported as market adjusted but trading costs are not explicitly calculated for the strategy.
For traders: Individuals acting as liquidity providers to institutions may earn small short term excess returns by buying after price drops and selling after price rises, but these profits are likely eroded by transaction costs for retail traders who cannot access the necessary data to identify 'intense' imbalances.
For the app: The app should flag stocks where retail order flow shows a sharp reversal (intense buying after a drop or selling after a rise) as potential short term mean reversion candidates, but must warn that the signal requires granular order flow data to be reliable and may be too small to cover retail trading costs.

[P5978] The Long‐Run Stock Returns Following Bond Ratings Changes (Ilia D. Dichev, Joseph D. Piotroski, 2001, The Journal of Finance, cited by 607, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00322
Question: How much of a bond rating downgrade is priced into stock prices on the announcement day versus over the following months and years, and does this underreaction persist after controlling for earnings surprises?
Data: US stock market (NYSE, AMEX, Nasdaq), 1970 to 1997, sample of 4,727 Moody's bond rating changes (including small and low credit quality firms), data from CRSP, COMPUSTAT, and Moody's Manuals.
Method: The authors calculate buy and hold abnormal returns (BHAR) and cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) for stocks following bond rating upgrades and downgrades. They match each firm to a benchmark portfolio based on size and book to market ratio to isolate the abnormal return. They test horizons of 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years. They also split the sample by firm size (large/small), credit quality (investment grade/non investment grade), and whether the downgrade was preceded by positive or negative earnings surprises.
Findings:
  * Following bond downgrades, stocks underperform by 10% to 14% in the first year (abnormal returns), with the underperformance persisting for up to three years.
  * The underperformance is most pronounced for small, low credit quality (non investment grade) firms, with a mean one year cumulative abnormal return of -21% for this subgroup.
  * There are no reliable abnormal returns following bond rating upgrades; the returns are close to zero across all time horizons.
  * The negative returns following downgrades occur even when the downgrade is preceded by positive earnings surprises, suggesting the market underreacts specifically to the rating change itself rather than just the earnings news.
  * The underperformance is observed in 26 out of 28 calendar years in the sample, indicating the effect is persistent and not limited to a specific economic period.
Strength: strong (The study uses a comprehensive sample of nearly all available Moody's ratings changes over 28 years, includes small and underfollowed firms often excluded in prior research, and rigorously controls for size, book to market, and earnings surprises.)
Limits: The data is limited to the US market from 1970 to 1997; the study does not report transaction costs or the feasibility of shorting small, illiquid stocks; the sample excludes firms without size/book to market data which might have had even worse returns.
For traders: Individual traders should be cautious about holding stocks that receive a bond rating downgrade, as the market tends to underreact, leading to continued price declines over the next 12 months, especially for smaller companies.
For the app: The app should flag any stock receiving a bond rating downgrade as a high probability 'negative storyline' trigger, predicting a continued decline over the next 12 months, and specifically highlight if the firm is small or has low credit quality.

[P5981] Investor Reaction to Salient News in Closed‐End Country Funds (Peter Klibanoff, Owen A Lamont, Thierry A. Wizman, 1998, The Journal of Finance, cited by 432, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.265570
Question: How does salient news affect the speed at which closed end fund prices adjust to their net asset value?
Data: 39 closed end country funds, 25 countries, US listed, 1986 through March 1994, 9781 fund week observations, weekly data
Method: Compare price elasticity to net asset value changes in weeks with front page New York Times news versus weeks without news
Findings:
  * In typical weeks, price elasticity to net asset value is 0.50 (Table III, Column 4), indicating underreaction
  * In weeks with front page New York Times news, price elasticity is closer to one (Abstract)
  * Trading volume is 41 percent higher in news weeks (Table V, Column 1)
  * Abnormal volume is associated with greater price reaction to net asset value (Table VII discussion)
  * Results hold across emerging and established markets (Table VI snippet)
Strength: strong (Large sample size (9781 observations), published in top finance journal, clear econometric method)
Limits: Data ends in 1994 (old), focuses on closed end funds not regular stocks, no explicit trading strategy returns or costs reported, some text sections omitted
For traders: Prices often move slower than fundamentals, but catch up quickly when major news hits; gaps between price and value may close faster during news events
For the app: Flag when a stock has a fundamental change but price hasn't moved much (underreaction), but warn that if major news hits, the gap closes fast

[P5984] Of Shepherds, Sheep, and the Cross-autocorrelations in Equity Returns (Swaminathan G. Badrinath, Jayant Raghunath Kale, Thomas H. Noe, 1995, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 331, read from: abstract and citing papers)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/8.2.401
Question: Do stocks held by informed institutional investors lead the price movements of stocks held by uninformed retail investors, and can this delay be traded?
Data: US stock market, sample period 1981-1988 (based on citing paper 'Information Efficiency of U.S. Restaurant Stocks...'), portfolios formed by institutional ownership levels.
Method: The authors sort stocks into portfolios based on the level of institutional ownership. They then test if the past returns of the 'high institutional ownership' portfolio predict (lead) the current returns of the 'low institutional ownership' portfolio, controlling for firm size.
Findings:
  * Returns on the portfolio of stocks with the highest level of institutional ownership lead the returns on portfolios of stocks with lower levels of institutional ownership.
  * This lead lag effect persists even after firm size is controlled for.
  * The effect is apparent at longer lags than the size related lag effects documented in earlier research (Lo and MacKinlay, 1990).
  * Citing papers note that high institutional ownership portfolios generally have higher Sharpe ratios than low ownership portfolios within size quartiles.
  * Citing papers confirm that information travels more quickly for stocks with high institutional ownership, causing them to lead stocks with low ownership.
Strength: moderate (The paper provides a clear economic mechanism and empirical evidence, but the specific sample period (1981-1988) is old, and detailed return numbers are not available in the provided text.)
Limits: The provided text is only the abstract and second hand citations; specific return percentages, exact lag durations (in days), and transaction cost estimates are not reported. The primary data sample is from 1981-1988, which may not reflect modern market conditions.
For traders: An individual trader might attempt to buy stocks with low institutional ownership after seeing a price move in a related stock with high institutional ownership, but the specific profit potential after costs is unknown from this text.
For the app: The app should flag 'leader' stocks (high institutional ownership) and monitor 'follower' stocks (low institutional ownership) in the same industry or supply chain, alerting the user when the leader moves but the follower has not yet reacted.

[P5985] Investor and Analyst Reactions to Earnings Announcements of Related Firms: An Empirical Analysis (Sundaresh Ramnath, 2002, Journal of Accounting Research, cited by 307, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679x.t01-1-00057
Question: Do investors and analysts underreact to earnings news from the first company in an industry to report, causing predictable price drifts for other companies in the same sector that report later?
Data: US stock market, firm quarters from 1995 to 1997 (sample size 2,247), data from I/B/E/S for forecasts and CRSP for returns.
Method: The study identifies the first company in an industry to announce earnings. It calculates the forecast error (surprise) and the stock return of this first announcer. It then uses a regression model to predict the likely forecast errors for other companies in the same industry that have not yet reported. It measures the stock returns of these 'subsequent announcers' over a window starting two days after the first announcement and ending the day after their own earnings report.
Findings:
  * Subsequent announcers earn a mean market adjusted return of 0.42% over an average holding period of 7 trading days (1995-1997).
  * The 0.42% return over 7 days translates to roughly 15% on an annualized basis.
  * Returns are positive and significant in 10 out of 11 quarters tested.
  * About 65% of the total abnormal return occurs specifically around the subsequent announcer's own earnings announcement date.
  * Strategies based on the first announcer's stock return (CARFA) or raw forecast error (PFEFA) yield significant positive returns, while strategies based on the predicted forecast error (PPFE) show mixed results in regression but positive returns in portfolio tests.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a clear holdout sample and robust statistical tests, but the sample is limited to three years (1995-1997) and does not account for transaction costs.)
Limits: The study only covers 1995-1997; returns are not adjusted for transaction costs; the strategy relies on paid I/B/E/S forecast data; the 'annualized' return assumes the strategy can be executed every week of the year, which is not possible as earnings are seasonal.
For traders: An individual trader can potentially profit by buying stocks of companies in the same industry as a 'good news' first announcer, holding them until their own earnings report, but must account for the cost of expensive analyst forecast data and trading fees.
For the app: The app should flag 'subsequent announcers' in an industry immediately after the first company reports a surprise, predicting the direction of the drift and setting a holding period until the second company's own earnings date.

[P5986] Underreaction to Self-Selected News Events: The Case of Stock Splits (David L. Ikenberry, Sundaresh Ramnath, 2002, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 272, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/15.2.489
Question: Do stock markets underreact to stock split announcements, leading to positive price drifts in the year following the event?
Data: US markets (NYSE, ASE, NASDAQ), sample of 3,000+ stock splits announced between 1988 and 1997, with return data through 1998; also extended historical sample from 1930 to 1987.
Method: The authors matched each splitting firm with a control firm based on market capitalization, value/growth ratio, momentum, and nominal share price. They calculated the difference in buy and hold returns between the split firm and its match over one year to measure abnormal drift.
Findings:
  * Mean match adjusted abnormal return of 9.00% (t=7.93) in the year following a split announcement (1988-1997).
  * Median abnormal one year return of 6.31% (p<.0001), indicating the drift is not driven by a few extreme outliers.
  * Abnormal returns were highest in high momentum quintiles (10.28% and 10.12% for quintiles 4 and 5).
  * Analysts underestimated earnings for splitting firms by -7.67% just before the split and only revised to -7.08% immediately after, showing sluggish expectation updates.
  * Calendar time arbitrage portfolios (long split firms, short matches) showed abnormal returns of roughly 8.8% per year (equal weighted) and 7% per year (value weighted) for the 1988-1997 period.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large sample size, rigorous matching controls for size, value, momentum, and price, and validates findings across multiple time periods (1930s-1990s) and estimation methods.)
Limits: The primary data sample ends in 1997, so there is no direct evidence in this paper regarding performance after the year 2000; transaction costs are not explicitly quantified in the text.
For traders: A trader could potentially capture a ~9% annual return by buying stocks immediately after they announce a split, but this requires holding for a full year and may be eroded by trading costs.
For the app: Add a 'Split Announcement' event trigger that flags stocks for a potential long term hold storyline, specifically monitoring for sluggish analyst earnings revisions as a confirmation signal.

Themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not

[P5990] The Cost of Institutional Equity Trades (Donald B. Keim, Ananth Madhavan, 1998, Financial Analysts Journal, cited by 260, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v54.n4.2198
Question: What are the magnitude and determinants of trading costs for institutional equity trades, and how do these costs vary by trade size, market capitalization, and investment style?
Data: U.S. equity markets (NYSE, Amex, Nasdaq); Sample of 21 institutional traders; Period: January 1991 to March 1993; Data source: Detailed transaction level data from institutional traders (Lexus Group/SEI Corporation type data, not public databases).
Method: The authors analyze a large sample of institutional trades to decompose costs into explicit (commissions) and implicit (price impact, opportunity cost) components. They regress these costs against variables like trade size (relative to outstanding shares), market capitalization, stock price, and investment style (value, technical, index) to determine how costs vary systematically.
Findings:
  * For exchange listed stocks, the average total round trip cost for the smallest market cap quintile is 3.81 percent, while for the largest quintile it is 0.57 percent.
  * Commission costs for institutional investors averaged about 0.20 percent of trade value in the 1991-93 period, down from 0.58 percent in 1982.
  * Round trip trading costs vary significantly by investment style: value managers averaged 0.45 percent, index managers 1.09 percent, and momentum (technical) traders 2.04 percent.
  * For Nasdaq stocks, total trading costs are generally higher than for exchange listed stocks, with the smallest market cap quintile reaching 2.85 percent for buyers and 2.91 percent for sellers.
  * Sell costs generally exceed buy costs; for example, the largest trade size quartile for exchange listed stocks had a total cost of 0.90 percent for buys but 1.42 percent for sells.
Strength: strong (The study uses high quality, detailed transaction level data from a large sample of 21 institutions, allowing for precise measurement of both explicit and implicit costs that public data cannot provide.)
Limits: The data is from 1991-1993, which may not reflect current market structures (e.g., high frequency trading, decimalization, dark pools); the sample is limited to institutional trades, which may not perfectly mirror retail execution costs; the paper does not test if specific trading signals generate returns after costs, only the cost of executing trades.
For traders: Individual traders should expect significantly higher costs for small cap stocks and for strategies requiring immediate execution (like momentum), whereas patient, fundamental based strategies on large cap stocks incur much lower costs.
For the app: The app should include a 'Cost Estimator' feature that adjusts expected returns based on the stock's market cap and the user's intended holding period/aggressiveness, warning that small cap or rapid turnover strategies may be eaten up by transaction costs.
Themes: From signal to trade

[P6039] More Than Words: Quantifying Language to Measure Firms' Fundamentals (Paul C. Tetlock, Maytal Saar‐Tsechansky, Sofus A. Macskassy, 2008, The Journal of Finance, cited by 2,307, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01362.x
Question: Does the fraction of negative words in financial news stories predict firm earnings and stock returns over short horizons, and is this effect driven by underreaction to fundamental news?
Data: US market (S&P 500 firms), 1980 to 2004, 980 qualifying firms, data from Dow Jones News Service (DJNS) and Wall Street Journal (WSJ) via Factiva, matched to CRSP.
Method: The authors quantify news tone by calculating the fraction of negative words in stories using the Harvard IV-4 dictionary. They test if this predicts future earnings and if stocks underreact to negative news by forming daily long short portfolios (buying firms with positive news, shorting those with negative news) and holding for one day, then rebalancing. They also test if stories containing the word stem 'earn' show stronger effects.
Findings:
  * Negative words in news stories forecast low firm earnings in the next quarter.
  * Stock prices briefly underreact to negative words; the market reaction to DJNS stories persists beyond the first day, with 6.2 basis points of the reaction occurring after day 2.
  * A long short strategy (long positive news, short negative news) based on DJNS stories earned an average risk adjusted return (alpha) of 10.31 basis points per day (1980-2004) before costs.
  * The strategy's annualized raw return was 21.07% before costs, but dropped to -4.37% after assuming 10 basis points in round trip transaction costs.
  * The predictive power of negative words is strongest for stories that focus on fundamentals (those containing the word stem 'earn').
Strength: strong (The study uses a long sample period (25 years), rigorous risk adjustment (Fama French and Carhart factors), and explicitly tests the impact of transaction costs, though the sample is limited to S&P 500 firms.)
Limits: The strategy is only profitable before transaction costs; with realistic costs (e.g., 10 bps), it loses money. The sample is restricted to S&P 500 firms (large caps) and ends in 2004, so it does not test if the effect persists in recent years or for smaller stocks.
For traders: While negative news tone predicts lower future returns, the short term underreaction is too small to overcome trading costs for a simple daily rebalancing strategy on large cap stocks.
For the app: The app should flag stories with high negative word fractions, especially those mentioning 'earnings' or fundamentals, as potential signals of underreaction, but must warn users that the immediate price drift is likely too small to trade profitably after costs without further refinement.

[P6046] Wisdom of Crowds: The Value of Stock Opinions Transmitted Through Social Media (Hailiang Chen, Prabuddha De, Yu Jeffrey Hu et al., 2014, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 1,245, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhu001
Question: Do investor opinions on social media (Seeking Alpha) predict stock returns and earnings surprises?
Data: US stocks, 2005-2012, Seeking Alpha articles/comments, CRSP/Compustat, IBES
Method: Textual analysis of negative word frequency in articles and comments to predict abnormal returns over 3 months and earnings surprises
Findings:
  * 1% higher negative words in SA articles predicts 0.25% to 0.28% lower abnormal returns over 3 months
  * 1% higher negative words in SA comments predicts 0.16% lower abnormal returns over 3 months
  * Long short portfolio (quintile based on article tone) earns 2.6 basis points daily abnormal return

Limits: Sample ends in 2012; data access for Seeking Alpha history may be difficult now; transaction costs not calculated; specific earnings surprise prediction numbers not provided in text
For traders: Sentiment from retail investors on SA can signal underperformance if negative tone is high, but returns are small and data access is hard

[P6056] Inter-firm linkages and the wealth effects of financial distress along the supply chain☆ (Michael G. Hertzel, Z LI, M OFFICER et al., 2007, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 755, read from: citing papers only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2007.01.005
Question: How do stock prices of suppliers and customers react to a major customer's financial distress or bankruptcy, and over what time horizon?
Data: US stock market, 250 firms filing for bankruptcy between 1981 and 2004; data from bankruptcy filings and stock returns (second hand report from citing papers).
Method: The study identifies customers that filed for bankruptcy and measures the stock price reaction of their suppliers and other customers around the filing date and pre filing distress dates.
Findings:
  * The mean stock market reaction to suppliers of firms filing for bankruptcy is –1.96%.
  * The mean stock market reaction to customers of firms filing for bankruptcy is –0.19%.
  * Suppliers experience significantly negative stock returns around the bankruptcy filing date of a distressed customer.
  * Long term horizontal alliance partners experience a cumulative abnormal return (CAR) of -2% over the window (-1, +1) days.
  * Suppliers experience average CARs ranging from –0.61% to –2.73% when customers announce the replacement of their CEOs.
Strength: moderate (Large sample of 250 bankruptcy events over 23 years, but findings are reported second hand without access to the original regression tables or cost data.)
Limits: Data is entirely second hand from citing papers; no original text available to verify exact holding periods, transaction costs, or whether returns are risk adjusted; sample ends in 2004, so recent performance is unknown; specific entry/exit rules for trading are not detailed in the citations.
For traders: Suppliers of distressed customers tend to drop in value quickly (within 1-3 days) when the customer files for bankruptcy or shows early signs of trouble, offering a short term shorting opportunity.
For the app: The app should flag suppliers of any company showing 'pre filing distress' (defined as the day of the largest negative return in the prior year) and suggest a short position with a 1-3 day holding period.

[P6057] Sources of gains in horizontal mergers: evidence from customer, supplier, and rival firms (C. Edward Fee, Shawn Thomas, 2004, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 704, read from: citing papers only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2003.10.002
Question: When two firms in the same industry merge, how do the stock prices of their rivals, customers, and suppliers react in the short term, and what does this imply about the source of merger gains (efficiency vs. market power)?
Data: US stock market, 1980 to 1997, large sample of public horizontal mergers; data source is Compustat segment files and CRSP (inferred from citing papers describing the methodology).
Method: Event study measuring Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CAR) around the merger announcement date for three groups: firms competing with the merger (rivals), firms buying from the merger (customers), and firms selling to the merger (suppliers).
Findings:
  * Rival firms saw a positive stock price reaction of 0.24% over the 3-day window centered on the announcement (CAR(-1, 1)).
  * Customer firms showed no statistically significant change in stock prices (CAR was insignificant) around the announcement.
  * Supplier firms experienced a negative market reaction of -0.30% following horizontal merger announcements.
  * The results support the 'efficiency hypothesis' (mergers create value through productivity) rather than the 'market power hypothesis' (mergers create value by raising prices), as rivals gained while customers did not lose.
  * The study identified 39 public horizontal mergers that were challenged by antitrust regulators, using joint annual reports to verify these cases.
Strength: moderate (The study uses a large historical sample (1980-1997) and established data matching procedures, but the specific return numbers cited here come from second hand summaries in later papers, not the original full text.)
Limits: Data is second hand (from citing papers only); the original paper text is not available to verify exact sample sizes, cost assumptions, or holding periods beyond the event window. The findings are specific to US horizontal mergers from 1980-1997.
For traders: This suggests that when a merger is announced, buying competitors (rivals) and shorting suppliers might be a viable short term strategy, but buying customers is unlikely to yield immediate returns.
For the app: The app should flag 'Rival' and 'Supplier' stocks immediately upon a merger announcement, assigning a 'Buy' signal to rivals and a 'Sell' signal to suppliers, while ignoring customers for short term trades.

[P6065] Bankruptcy spillover effects on strategic alliance partners (Audra L. Boone, Vladimir I. Ivanov, 2011, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 151, read from: citing papers only)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2011.10.003
Question: How do stock prices of strategic alliance partners react to a partner's bankruptcy filing, and can this reaction be traded?
Data: US stock market, sample period not reported in citing papers, data source: SDC Platinum for alliance identification (implied by citations), sample size not reported in citing papers.
Method: Identify firms with strategic alliances. When one partner files for bankruptcy, measure the stock price reaction of the non bankrupt partner around the announcement date and track performance over the following two years.
Findings:
  * Non bankrupt strategic alliance partners experience a negative stock price reaction around the partner's bankruptcy filing announcement.
  * The bankruptcy of a partner leads to a decrease in the non bankrupt partner's profit margins and investment levels over the subsequent two years.
  * The negative spillover effect is more severe for partnerships that are longer in duration and closer in nature.
  * The negative impact on stock prices and performance is insignificant for joint venture partners, unlike strategic alliance partners.
  * Terminating the alliance with a bankrupt partner can alleviate the negative spillover effects on the non bankrupt firm.
Strength: moderate (The findings are consistently cited across many papers, but specific return magnitudes, holding periods, and cost adjustments are not provided in the second hand summaries.)
Limits: Data is entirely second hand from citing papers; exact return percentages, specific holding periods for the initial reaction, transaction costs, and sample years are not reported. The distinction between 'strategic alliances' and 'joint ventures' is critical but definitions may vary.
For traders: If a company you hold has a strategic alliance, a bankruptcy filing by the partner is a strong sell signal, but the effect may be less severe or non existent if the relationship is a formal joint venture.
For the app: Add a 'Counterparty Risk' module that flags stocks with strategic alliances; if a partner files for bankruptcy, trigger a 'Sell' or 'Reduce Position' alert, but suppress this alert if the relationship is classified as a Joint Venture.

[P6103] The Importance of Industry Links in Merger Waves (Kenneth Robinson Ahern, Jarrad Harford, 2013, The Journal of Finance, cited by 494, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12122
Question: How do merger waves propagate through customer supplier industry networks, and what are the time delays for these waves to reach connected versus distant industries?
Data: US market, 471 industries, sample period 1986 to 2010, data from Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) input output tables and SDC merger database.
Method: The authors model the economy as a network of industries connected by trade flows. They measure the 'distance' between industries based on the strength of these links. They then track merger activity over time to see if a surge in mergers in one industry predicts a surge in connected industries in the following years, comparing the speed of transmission through supplier links versus customer links.
Findings:
  * Merger activity transmits to close industries quickly (within one year) and to distant industries with a delay of two to three years.
  * Merger activity in close industries leads to increased activity in the following year, while distant industries see increased activity in two or three years.
  * Shocks travel faster through supplier links than through customer links because the supplier network is more densely connected.
  * Industries that are more central in the product market network are more likely to experience merger waves during economy wide surges.
  * Industry pairs with strong customer supplier connections have an average of 12.5 mergers over the sample period, compared to 0.11 for pairs with no meaningful connection.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large sample of 51,002 mergers over 24 years and detailed, high quality input output data to establish a robust network structure.)
Limits: The paper analyzes merger waves at the industry level, not individual stock prices; it does not report trading returns, holding periods for stocks, or transaction costs, and focuses on the US market only.
For traders: This paper suggests that news of a merger wave in a specific industry (e.g., sawmills) can serve as a leading indicator for merger activity in connected industries (e.g., pulp mills) 1 to 3 years later, but it does not provide a direct strategy for buying individual stocks to profit from this delay.
For the app: The app should map user selected stocks to their industry's position in the customer supplier network and alert the user if a merger wave begins in a 'hub' or 'supplier' industry, predicting a potential wave in the user's stock's industry 1-3 years out.

[P6117] The Value of Investment Banking Relationships: Evidence from the Collapse of Lehman Brothers (Chitru S. Fernando, ANTHONY D. MAY, William L. Megginson, 2012, The Journal of Finance, cited by 138, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2011.01711.x
Question: How did the stock prices of companies linked to Lehman Brothers through specific investment banking services react to Lehman's collapse, and does the strength of that link predict the size of the loss?
Data: US stock market, 1998-2008 sample period, event window centered on September 15, 2008. Sample includes 184 equity underwriting clients, 53 debt underwriting clients, 87 M&A clients, 151 NYSE specialist clients, and 633 analyst coverage clients. Data sources: SEC filings, CRSP, Compustat, and Thomson CDS/Spectrum.
Method: The authors measured the stock price reaction (abnormal returns) of client firms over short windows (1 to 7 days) and medium windows (up to 30 days) surrounding Lehman's bankruptcy. They compared these returns against a control group of clients from similar investment banks that did not fail. They also ran regressions to see if the number of past deals or firm size changed the reaction.
Findings:
  * Equity underwriting clients lost an average of -4.85% over the 7-day window (-5 to +1) surrounding the bankruptcy, which was significantly worse than the -1.91% loss of clients from similar banks.
  * On the day of the bankruptcy (Day 0), equity underwriting clients dropped -1.48% (equally weighted) or -1.76% (value weighted) in abnormal returns.
  * Over the 30-day period following the event (+2 to +30), equity underwriting clients continued to underperform, losing an additional -7.07% in abnormal returns compared to the control group.
  * Firms with stronger relationships (more past equity offerings with Lehman) suffered larger losses; the reaction was also worse for smaller, younger, and financially constrained companies.
  * Clients of other services (debt underwriting, M&A, NYSE specialist, analyst coverage) showed no significant negative reaction in the short term unless they also had an equity underwriting relationship.
Strength: strong (The study uses a unique natural experiment (Lehman's sudden failure) with a large sample size, rigorous statistical controls (Fama French Carhart model), and robustness checks against alternative explanations like liquidity shifts.)
Limits: The results are specific to the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of a single major bank; it is unclear if this 'contagion' effect applies to smaller bank failures or non financial shocks. The study measures reaction to a specific event, not a repeatable trading strategy for future news.
For traders: When a major financial partner (like a lead underwriter) fails, the market punishes their equity clients immediately and for weeks; however, this is a one time event study, not a repeatable signal for trading other news.
For the app: Add a 'Relationship Risk' metric that flags stocks where a major service provider (underwriter, lender, or advisor) is in distress; if that provider fails, the app should predict a multi week negative drift for the client.

[P6146] Contagion and competitive intra-industry effects of bankruptcy announcements (Larry H.P. Lang, René M. Stulz, 1992, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 920, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405x(92)90024-r
Question: How do bankruptcy announcements of one firm affect the stock prices of its competitors, and does this effect depend on industry leverage and concentration?
Data: US stock market, 1970 to 1989, 59 bankruptcy announcements of firms with >$120M liabilities, data from COMPUSTAT and CRSP
Method: The authors form value weighted portfolios of competitors (firms with the same 4-digit SIC code) for each bankruptcy event. They calculate abnormal returns (returns above what the market model predicts) for an 11-day window centered on the announcement. They then split these portfolios into groups based on industry leverage (high vs. low debt to assets) and industry concentration (Herfindahl index) to see if the reaction differs.
Findings:
  * On average, a value weighted portfolio of competitors loses 1% in value on the day of the bankruptcy announcement.
  * For industries with high leverage (debt to assets above the sample median of 0.22), competitor equity falls by 2.87% (significant at 0.01 level).
  * For industries with low leverage, the abnormal return is positive but not statistically significant.
  * In highly concentrated industries with low leverage, competitor equity increases by 2.2%.
  * In highly concentrated industries with high leverage, competitors lose 3.22% (significant at 0.01 level).
Strength: moderate (The study uses a large sample of 59 events over 20 years and rigorous statistical controls, but the sample is limited to large US firms and a specific historical period.)
Limits: The sample only covers US firms with over $120 million in liabilities from 1970-1989; it does not test if these returns persist after transaction costs or in modern markets; the holding period is strictly an 11-day event window, not a multi week strategy.
For traders: A retail trader could potentially profit by shorting competitors in highly leveraged industries when a bankruptcy is announced, or buying competitors in concentrated, low leverage industries, but must act quickly as the price reaction happens within days.
For the app: The app should flag a bankruptcy event and automatically check the target industry's leverage and concentration metrics to predict whether competitors will likely drop (contagion) or rise (competitive gain) in the next few days.

Question: Do bankruptcy announcements of one company cause negative stock returns and wider credit spreads for its creditors?

Method: Event study measuring abnormal stock returns and CDS spread changes for creditors around bankruptcy dates

[P6167] Financial Firm Bankruptcy and Contagion (Jean Helwege, Gaiyan Zhang, 2015, European Finance Review, cited by 64, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rof/rfv045
Question: Do stock prices of rival firms and creditors of a financial firm drop significantly and persistently after a bankruptcy or distress announcement, and can this delay be traded over days to weeks?
Data: US and global financial firms, 1980-2010, sample of 142 bankruptcies and 149 distressed firms; data from bankruptcydata.com, Compustat, CRSP, and Epiq Systems.
Method: Event study measuring abnormal stock returns (CAR) of rival firms (same industry/state) and creditors (unsecured claimants) around the announcement date of bankruptcy or distress, using [-2, 2] and [-5, 5] day windows.
Findings:
  * Creditors suffered an average decline of -2.29% over the [-2, 2] window centered on the bankruptcy announcement (402 firms).
  * Rival firms in the same state and business line saw a -1.45% return over the [0, 1] window and sharper drops over longer windows.
  * Distress news caused larger contagion than bankruptcy filings: rivals of distressed firms saw a -2.06% return over the [-2, 2] window.
  * Lehman creditors fell 1.24% on average over [0, 1] and up to 3.87% over the 5-day window for those with largest exposures.
  * AIG creditors lost 4.24% over the 5-day announcement window, with some losing over 10% around the specific distress day in September 2008.
Strength: moderate (Large sample size (142 bankruptcies, 149 distress cases) and robust event study methodology, but limited to short windows (days) and specific to financial firms.)
Limits: Results are based on short event windows (up to 5 days); no data on returns over weeks or months; sample ends in 2010; effects are specific to financial firms and may not apply to non financial supply chains; costs are not calculated.
For traders: Shorting rivals or creditors immediately after news breaks yields small but significant losses for the target stocks, but the window is very short (days) and the magnitude is modest (1-4%) unless the firm is a major systemically important player like AIG.
For the app: Flag 'distress' news (not just bankruptcy) as a stronger signal for rival contagion; prioritize firms in the same state and business line; warn that the price drop usually happens within 1-2 days, not weeks.

[P6182] Overreaction, Delayed Reaction, and Contrarian Profits (Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Sheridan D. Titman, 1995, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 414, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/8.4.973
Question: Does the delay in stock prices reacting to common market factors (lead lag) or the overreaction to firm specific news drive short term contrarian profits?
Data: US markets (NYSE and AMEX), 1963 to 1990, sample of ~1,987 firms per week with at least 260 weeks of data, excluding stocks under $1, using CRSP daily return data.
Method: The authors decompose contrarian profits into two parts: one caused by some stocks reacting slower than others to market wide news (lead lag), and one caused by prices overreacting to company specific news and then correcting. They test this by regressing stock returns against current and lagged market index returns and by running specific trading strategies on size sorted portfolios.
Findings:
  * Lead lag structure (delayed reaction to common factors) contributes less than 5% of observed contrarian profits.
  * Overreaction to firm specific information accounts for approximately 105% of the total contrarian profits.
  * A weekly contrarian strategy on the full sample yields an average profit of 1.37% per week per dollar long.
  * For small firms, the lagged beta (delayed reaction to market) is 0.2350, while for large firms it is close to zero.
  * A contrarian strategy applied to 50 size sorted portfolios (designed to exploit lead lag) yields an average profit of -0.02%, effectively zero.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (1987 firms/week) over a long period (27 years) with rigorous statistical decomposition and robustness checks (e.g., skipping days, subsampling).)
Limits: Data is limited to US stocks (NYSE/AMEX) from 1963-1990; the paper does not report transaction costs or net returns after fees; the 'overreaction' finding is based on statistical residuals, not direct news sentiment analysis.
For traders: Trying to profit from the delay of one stock following another (lead lag) is unlikely to work; instead, short term profits come from betting against extreme moves caused by company specific news.
For the app: The app should prioritize identifying firm specific news over general market news when building storylines for short term trades, as market wide delays are too small to trade profitably.

[P6211] Momentum crashes (Kent Daniel, Tobias J. Moskowitz, 2016, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 880, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2015.12.002
Question: Do momentum strategies survive trading costs and recent market conditions, and can their crash risk be reduced by forecasting mean and variance?
Data: US equities (CRSP data), 1927-2013; also international markets (EU, UK, JP, Global) and other asset classes (commodities, currencies, bonds) from 1972-2013. Sample includes all NYSE, AMEX, NASDAQ common stocks with sufficient return history.
Method: The authors construct a static momentum strategy (buy past winners, sell past losers) and compare it to two dynamic versions: one that adjusts position size based on forecasts of future mean returns and volatility, and one that holds a constant volatility target. They test these strategies across different time periods, markets, and asset classes, specifically looking at performance during 'panic' states (market declines followed by rebounds).
Findings:
  * In the US sample (1927-2013), the static 'Winners Minus Losers' (WML) strategy had an annualized alpha of 22.3% and a Sharpe ratio of 0.71, but suffered severe crashes (e.g., 1932, 2009) where past losers outperformed past winners by large margins.
  * The dynamic momentum strategy, which scales exposure based on forecasts of mean and variance, achieved a Sharpe ratio nearly double that of the static strategy (approx. 1.19 vs 0.59 in the full sample) and significantly mitigated crash losses.
  * Momentum crashes occur specifically in 'panic' states: when the lagged two year market return is negative and the contemporaneous market return is positive (a rebound), often accompanied by high volatility.
  * The dynamic strategy outperformed the static strategy in all four quarter century subsamples (1927-1949, 1950-1974, 1975-1999, 2000-2013), including the period after the 2008 crisis.
  * Transaction costs are acknowledged as a factor: the dynamic strategy employs higher leverage and incurs higher trading costs than the static strategy, which must be considered in practical implementation.
Strength: strong (The study uses a very long historical sample (87 years) covering multiple crashes, tests across diverse international markets and asset classes, and validates the dynamic strategy using an out of sample expanding window approach.)
Limits: The paper does not provide specific net of cost return figures for the dynamic strategy; it explicitly states that actual implementation would incur higher transaction costs due to leverage and rebalancing. The 'panic' state definition relies on specific lagged market return and volatility thresholds that may vary in real time application.
For traders: A static momentum strategy is prone to severe, predictable crashes during market rebounds after long declines; traders should consider reducing or exiting momentum positions when the market has fallen significantly and volatility is high.
For the app: Implement a 'Panic State' detector that flags when the market has dropped over the last 2 years and is currently rebounding with high volatility; when triggered, the app should advise reducing momentum exposure or shorting the strategy to avoid the crash.
Method card: method: Static Momentum (12-1 month) | trigger: Rank all stocks by their cumulative returns from 12 months ago to 1 month ago (skipping the most recent month). | direction: both | entry: End of the formation month (after the 1-month skip). | holding_days: 21 (1 month, rebalanced monthly) | reported_return: 22.3% annualized alpha (US, 1927-2013); Sharpe ratio 0.71. | after_costs: not reported (paper notes costs are ignored in reported figures) | stocks: All NYSE, AMEX, NASDAQ common stocks with valid prices and 8+ monthly returns; value weighted portfolios. | market_years: US, 1927-2013 | still_works: mixed (works on average but suffers severe crashes in specific 'panic' states like 2009) | data_needed: Daily or monthly historical price data (free from CRSP/Yahoo Finance); requires 12+ months of history. | storyline_fit: Fits the 'past performance predicts future' storyline, but the app must warn that this link breaks during market rebounds after long declines. | retail_usable: maybe (high crash risk and shorting requirements make it difficult for casual traders without hedging tools) | asset_class: stocks
Method card: method: Dynamic Momentum (Mean Variance Forecasting) | trigger: Forecast the next month's mean return and variance of the momentum portfolio using lagged market returns, market volatility, and a 'bear market' indicator. | direction: both (position size varies, can go to zero or negative) | entry: End of the formation month, with weight adjusted by the forecast. | holding_days: 21 (1 month, rebalanced monthly) | reported_return: Sharpe ratio approx. 1.19 (scaled to 19% vol) vs 0.59 for static; alpha approximately doubled. | after_costs: no (paper states it incurs higher costs due to leverage and turnover, but does not quantify the net return) | stocks: Same universe as static strategy; weights adjusted dynamically. | market_years: US, 1927-2013 (tested out of sample); also robust in EU, UK, JP, Global markets. | still_works: yes (outperformed static strategy in all subsamples including 2000-2013) | data_needed: Historical price data for stocks and the market index; requires calculating volatility and regression coefficients (complex for retail). | storyline_fit: Perfect fit: the app can link the 'market decline + rebound + high volatility' event chain to a 'reduce momentum' signal, confirming the story that momentum crashes are forecastable. | retail_usable: no (requires complex forecasting models, leverage management, and shorting capabilities) | asset_class: stocks
Method card: method: Constant Volatility Momentum | trigger: Rebalance the static momentum portfolio monthly to maintain a constant target volatility (19% in the study). | direction: both (position size scaled to maintain volatility) | entry: End of the formation month, with weight adjusted to hit target volatility. | holding_days: 21 (1 month, rebalanced monthly) | reported_return: Sharpe ratio approx. 1.02 (scaled to 19% vol); better than static but worse than dynamic. | after_costs: no (paper implies higher costs than static due to leverage, but does not quantify net return) | stocks: Same universe as static strategy; weights adjusted dynamically. | market_years: US, 1927-2013; robust in international markets. | still_works: yes (outperformed static strategy in all subsamples) | data_needed: Historical price data to calculate rolling volatility; requires leverage adjustments. | storyline_fit: Good fit: the app can use volatility spikes as a trigger to reduce position size, linking 'high volatility' events to 'lower risk' actions. | retail_usable: maybe (simpler than dynamic forecasting but still requires leverage and shorting) | asset_class: stocks

[P6214] It Depends on Where You Search: Institutional Investor Attention and Underreaction to News (Azi Ben-Rephael, Zhi Da, Ryan D. Israelsen, 2017, Review of Financial Studies, cited by 714, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhx031
Question: Do stocks with earnings surprises or analyst recommendation changes that fail to attract institutional investor attention experience slower price adjustment (drift) over the following days compared to those that do attract attention?
Data: US stock market (CRSP data), sample covers earnings announcements and analyst recommendation changes. The paper uses Bloomberg terminal search/read data for institutional attention (AIA) and I/B/E/S for earnings surprises. Specific sample years are not explicitly stated in the provided text, though the study references data up to 2013 in examples and mentions a sample of 34,400 earnings observations.
Method: The authors construct a measure of Abnormal Institutional Attention (AIA) based on Bloomberg terminal activity. They sort stocks into two groups: those with an attention spike (AIA=1) and those without (AIA=0) on the day of a news event (earnings or analyst recommendation). They then measure the cumulative returns of these groups over 5 and 10 trading days following the event, comparing the drift in low attention stocks against high attention stocks using calendar time portfolios.
Findings:
  * For earnings announcements, the low attention portfolio (LS_AIA=0) generated a 5-day return of 0.95% (statistically significant), while the high attention portfolio (LS_AIA=1) generated only 0.29% (not statistically significant).
  * The difference in returns between low and high attention stocks (DIFF portfolio) for earnings announcements was 0.65% over 5 days and 0.91% over 10 days, both statistically significant.
  * For analyst recommendation changes, the low attention portfolio (LS_AIA=0) generated a 5-day return of 0.64% (statistically significant), while the high attention portfolio (LS_AIA=1) generated 0.19% (not statistically significant).
  * The difference in returns between low and high attention stocks (DIFF portfolio) for analyst recommendation changes was 0.45% over 5 days and 0.60% over 10 days, both statistically significant.
  * Institutional attention (AIA) is the primary driver of immediate price adjustment; when AIA is high, the post event drift disappears, whereas when AIA is low, the drift persists.
Strength: strong (The study uses a novel, direct measure of institutional attention (Bloomberg data) rather than proxies like volume, and employs rigorous calendar time portfolio testing to isolate the drift effect.)
Limits: The provided text does not specify the exact start and end years of the full sample, nor does it report transaction costs or liquidity constraints for the trading strategies. The data source (Bloomberg terminal activity) is proprietary and not available to the public.
For traders: Individual traders can exploit the 'underreaction' in stocks where major news (earnings or analyst changes) occurs but fails to trigger a spike in institutional search activity; these stocks tend to drift in the direction of the news for 5-10 days.
For the app: The app should flag news events where the 'Institutional Attention' signal (modeled via search volume proxies if Bloomberg data is unavailable) is low relative to the magnitude of the news, predicting a multi day drift in the direction of the surprise.

Bloomberg data is paid; retail proxies (Google Trends) are free. | storyline_fit: Links the 'Event' (Earnings) to the 'Outcome' (Drift) only when the 'Reaction' (Institutional Attention) is missing, creating a clear 'Wait and See' storyline. | retail_usable: maybe, because the specific institutional data (Bloomberg) is unavailable, but retail attention proxies (Google Trends) might serve as a negative signal if they are low while news is high. | asset_class: stocks

[P6243] Shared analyst coverage: Unifying momentum spillover effects (Usman Ali, David A. Hirshleifer, 2019, Journal of Financial Economics, cited by 276, read from: full text (OpenAlex repository))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.10.007
Question: Do stock price movements of companies linked by shared analyst coverage predict future returns of those linked companies better than other linkage measures (like industry or supply chain), and can this be traded over a one month horizon?
Data: US stock market (1984-2015), International developed markets (various start dates to 2015), Sample includes stocks with analyst forecast data (IBES) and return data (S&P Capital IQ/AQR).
Method: The authors construct a 'Connected Stock' (CS) portfolio for each firm, consisting of other firms covered by the same analysts. They weight these connected firms by the number of shared analysts. They then sort all stocks into quintiles based on the past one month return of their specific CS portfolio. They buy the top quintile (high past CS return) and short the bottom quintile (low past CS return), holding for one month. They compare this to similar strategies using industry, geography, supply chain, and technology links.
Findings:
  * The CS momentum long short strategy generates a monthly five factor alpha of 1.19% (value weighted) and 2.10% (equal weighted) in the US (1984-2015).
  * The CS momentum factor subsumes other momentum effects: when controlling for CS momentum, the alphas of industry, geographic, customer, and technology momentum factors become insignificant or negative.
  * In international developed markets, the CS momentum factor generates a significant five factor alpha of 1.15% per month on average, while industry momentum alpha drops to 0.69% and often becomes insignificant after controlling for CS.
  * The effect persists in the recent sub sample (2000-2015), yielding a five factor alpha of 1.13% per month, though it is weaker than in the earlier period.
  * The one month strategy has a turnover of 313% per month, implying a break even transaction cost of 42.5 basis points, which is lower than average US transaction costs reported in other studies.
Strength: strong (The study uses a large, long term sample (1984-2015) across US and international markets, employs rigorous factor models (5-factor), and demonstrates that the effect is robust to controlling for other known anomalies and persists in recent data.)
Limits: The paper does not provide specific holding periods other than the monthly rebalance; it does not report raw returns net of explicit trading costs (only a break even estimate); the 'shared analyst' data is typically expensive and not available to casual retail traders; the effect is weaker in the 2000-2015 period compared to earlier years.
For traders: A trader can potentially profit by buying stocks whose linked peers (via shared analysts) have recently performed well and shorting those whose peers have performed poorly, holding for one month, but must manage high turnover and access expensive analyst coverage data.
For the app: The app should prioritize 'shared analyst' links over simple industry or geographic links when building storylines, as this linkage captures the strongest momentum spillover; it should flag stocks where the 'connected portfolio' has moved significantly in the last month as potential entry points.
Also tests (no cards written): Combined Linkage Momentum (1-month holding); Text based Industry Momentum (1-month holding); Alternative Geographic Momentum (State level, 1-month holding); Israelsen Network Momentum (1-month holding)

[P6261] Lazy Prices (Lauren H. Cohen, Christopher J. Malloy, Quoc Hung Nguyen, 2020, The Journal of Finance, cited by 388, read from: full text (your PDF, working paper version))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12885
Question: Do changes in filing text similarity predict future stock returns?
Data: US stocks, 1995-2014, SEC 10-K/10-Q filings
Method: Compare text similarity of current filing to prior year/quarter. Sort into quintiles. Long high similarity (non changers), Short low similarity (changers).
Findings:
  * Long non changers/Short changers earns 34-58 basis points per month (value weighted)
  * No immediate price reaction at filing release
  * The main return accrues gradually over the following 6 months and keeps accruing out to 18 months, with no reversal
  * Risk Factors section changes alone reach up to 188 basis points per month (5 factor alpha, equally weighted, t = 2.76): a section result, not the main return
  * Shorting fees for the changers (the short side) average about 72 basis points, lower than for the middle quintiles (80 to 92) (Characteristics of Quintile Portfolios; the table does not say over what period). The authors conclude that limits to arbitrage are not a significant contributor: turnover is modest, value weighted returns are a bit larger than equally weighted, and returns accrue slowly over 6 months
Strength: strong (Universe of US firms, 20 years of data, controls for risk factors)
Limits: Sample ends 2014, no post 2014 test; returns are before trading costs
For traders: Filing changes predict returns over 6 months, mostly on large diversified portfolios with modest turnover; returns are before costs, but the authors find the short side is not unusually costly to short
For the app: Monitor 10-K/10-Q text similarity, especially Risk Factors, to flag early warning signals

[P6294] When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10‐Ks (Tim Loughran B, Bill McDonald, 2011, The Journal of Finance, cited by 5,968, read from: full text (your PDF))
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01625.x
Question: Do financial specific negative, uncertainty, and modal word lists in 10-K filings predict stock returns around the filing date better than general purpose dictionaries?
Data: US stock market (CRSP/Compustat), 50,115 firm year 10-K filings from 1994 to 2008.
Method: The authors compare the predictive power of a new financial negative word list (Fin Neg) and other financial specific lists (uncertainty, modal strong, modal weak) against the standard Harvard dictionary. They sort firms into quintiles based on the proportion of these words in their 10-Ks and calculate the 4-day buy and hold excess return (days 0 to 3 relative to filing) for each group. They also run multivariate regressions controlling for size, book to market, and other factors.
Findings:
  * Using the Harvard dictionary (H4N Inf), sorting firms by negative word count produced no discernable pattern in 4-day excess returns (correlation -0.004).
  * Using the new Fin Neg list, firms with a high proportion of negative words had sharply negative median returns, while those with low proportions had slightly negative returns, creating a strong monotonic pattern (correlation -0.021).
  * In multivariate regressions, the Fin Neg list coefficient was -19.538 (t stat -2.64) for the 4-day excess return, whereas the Harvard list was -7.422 (t stat -1.35) and statistically insignificant.
  * The uncertainty list (Fin Unc) and modal word lists (strong and weak) also showed statistically significant negative coefficients (-42.026, -149.658, and -60.230 respectively) in regressions against 4-day excess returns.
  * The MD&A section alone did not produce tone measures with a more discernable impact on returns than the full 10-K document.
Strength: strong (Large sample size (50k+ filings), use of a specific financial domain dictionary validated against market reactions, and robust multivariate controls.)
Limits: The study only measures returns over a 4-day window around the filing date; it does not test holding periods of weeks or months, nor does it report trading costs or whether the strategy works after 2008.
For traders: General negative word counts from standard dictionaries are noisy and useless for trading 10-Ks; you must use a financial specific dictionary to see if the tone predicts a price drop in the days immediately following the filing.
For the app: Implement the specific 'Fin Neg', 'Fin Unc', and 'Modal' word lists provided by Loughran and McDonald (available online) instead of generic sentiment tools; trigger a 'sell' or 'avoid' signal if a 10-K filing shows a high density of these specific words, expecting a price drop within 3 days of the filing.
Also tests (no cards written): 10-K Harvard IV-4 Negative tone (4-day filing window); 10-K Litigious tone (4-day filing window); 10-K Positive tone (4-day filing window); 10-K Fin Neg tone (tf.idf weighted, 4-day filing window); 10-K Fin Uncertainty tone (tf.idf weighted, 4-day filing window); 10-K Modal Strong tone (tf.idf weighted, 4-day filing window); 10-K Modal Weak tone (tf.idf weighted, 4-day filing window); 10-K Litigious tone (tf.idf weighted, 4-day filing window); 10-K Positive tone (tf.idf weighted, 4-day filing window); 10-K Fin Neg tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Fin Uncertainty tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Modal Strong tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Modal Weak tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Harvard IV-4 Negative tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Litigious tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Positive tone (MD&A section only, 4-day filing window); 10-K Fin Neg tone (predicting Standardized Unexpected Earnings); 10-K Harvard IV-4 Negative tone (predicting Standardized Unexpected Earnings)
